She said: Mr. Speaker, I want to begin debate on Bill C-222 by explaining to the House and to the viewing public the kind of tortuous process that a private members' bill goes through.
This bill was first put on the Order Paper over four years ago by the hon. Jim Manly, since retired, who was the member of Parliament for the then riding of Cowi-chan-Malahat-The Islands, portions of which are now in my riding of Saanich-Gulf Islands. It has been on the Order Paper for four years, and it has only now been drawn. For the people out there who wonder about the haste or the speed of government, they have cause to wonder.
The intent of Bill C-222, an act to amend the Fruit, Vegetables and Honey Act (country of origin), was to address what I consider a major flaw or an omission in that act that countries of origin be made clear.
My amendment is that no person shall sell or offer for sale any produce unless the country of origin is shown clearly and legibly on the produce or the packaging thereof or on a sign placed near the produce.
Not only is the private member's bill a tortuous process, but the way this bill has come forth is also somewhat tortured. Until the end of last week we did not know whether the Fruit, Vegetables and Honey Act actually existed or whether it had been repealed. There was conflicting opinion as to whether or not it existed. Just 10 minutes or 15 minutes ago the Clerk of the House of Commons approached me in the corridor and assured me that yes the bill that I was seeking to amend did exist. Therefore I do not have a procedural hurdle to go over.
I ask the indulgence of the House and of the viewing public because this is complex but it is important for people to understand the route of bills through all devices of the House and how we get to where we are.
Right now the Fruit, Vegetables and Honey Act, first passed in 1935, is in effect but on February 15, 1990 the government tabled the Miscellaneous Statute Law Amendment Act and referred the bill to that act. It has been put in a hopper. It is a house cleaning measure. It knows that it has the Canada Agricultural Products Act passed in August 1988, but as a means of trying to house clean the statutes the government has put the Fruit, Vegetables and Honey Act in the Miscellaneous Statute Law Amendment Act.
The intention was to repeal the Fruit, Vegetables and Honey Act and to give force of the bill to the Canada Agricultural Products Act. This is why there is confusion and this is why the Clerk of the House was good enough to confirm with me that there is a bill which I am now attempting to amend.
There were a number of people in the House who were asking me whether or not I was going to ask for unanimous consent to withdraw this bill, but I felt it was important to speak on it to let people know the kind of Byzantine structures that exist here. What I want in this bill, that is that no person shall sell or offer for sale any produce unless the country of origin is clearly or legibly shown, is important.

June 4, 1990
Private Members' Business
Canadian consumers want to know the country of origin of the produce they buy for a variety of reasons. I will get into those a little later. The state of flux that I refer to on the whole mess that we are dealing with will be absolutely gripping television. People will be sitting on the edge of their chairs for the rest of this hour making sure they know all they want to know about fruits, vegetables and honey.
Obviously the country of origin was a concern of the government. The new Canada Agricultural Products Act under Section 32(i) provided for a way of looking at country of origin, but it is far too weak for my liking. It says:
32.(i) providing for systems to ascertain the places of origin or destination of agricultural products;
We can see that the language is not quite as clear as what I have proposed in Bill C-222.1 think it is in need of clarification because there is a lot of confusion not just about the country of origin but also about the kind of regulations which attend that.
There is lack of clarity regarding regulations. First, as to fines in the original Fruit, Vegetables and Honey Act, there is provision for fines of up to $50 for violations of the act. That must really scare people away. Firms like Loblaws or Save-On-Foods in my riding must be really scared of a $50 fine if they do not label certain products. There is also confusion about the kinds of produce subject to the labelling requirement.
In the regulations there are 27 listed products, whereas the Minister's office states there are 29. We are talking about products available both in Canada and elsewhere, such as apples, apricots, asparagus, beets, Brussels sprouts, cabbage, cantaloup, greenhouse tomatoes, and so on. There are 27 products listed in the regulations and 29 according to the minister's office. Therefore Bill C-222 makes it clear that it is important for people to know the country of origin.
My former colleague, Jim Manly, was motivated to introduce this bill over four years ago for three very important reasons; health, politics and the environment. I am not trying to say there are artificial divisions between those three but I use them as categories for reasons which will become apparent.
Concerned Canadians want to know where their food is coming from. If they participate in a boycott of a product or country, it is important for them to be aware of its origin. If a store carried Chilean grapes labelled when the Chilean regime was particularly repressive people could opt not to purchase those grapes.
Political boycotts of products can only be successful if such products are clearly identified. The present set-up appears to be ad hoc at best. There are only 29 fruits and vegetables now required to be labelled. The 29 are all products which are also grown in Canada. Bill C-222 is an effort to broaden that list.
I want to go back for a moment to grapes. Grapes are an important example because it was not just Chilean grapes that people wanted to boycott, it was also California grapes. This is where the health and environmental questions come in. I think the grape example embodied all three reasons why naming country of origin is important.
Consumers are bombarded with information with respect to the harmful effects of pesticides and chemicals. In Tblare County in California, the heart of the grape-growing region, over five million pounds of toxic pesticides are used annually. It is estimated that this is only one-third of the annual amount used as growers are only required to register certain pesticides. Companies do have an obligation to ensure the safety of the products they produce, but, unfortunately, this is not always the case. I think history has confirmed that we cannot always depend on an agri-food company to give us all the information we require.
I want to give some startling statistics regarding the whole grape question. Since 1986 in the community of Earlimart, California, five children have been diagnosed with cancer. In McFarland, California, 14 children have been so diagnosed. State medical officials claim that these figures represent a percentage per capita which is 12 times higher than national standards. What is interesting about these sad cases of childhood cancer is that the parents of all of these children worked in the vineyards. Several of the mothers of these children were working in the vineyards while they were pregnant.
We have some rather horrific statistics and data to back up the concerns. Five compounds, captain, pyre-
June 4, 1990

thrum, methylbromide, dinoseb and phosdrin, have been targeted for immediate ban. All of them are still being used in Canada. Many of these compounds are carcinogenic and have been identified as being particularly harmful to children when they are still in the womb. Also, pesticide residue is likely to show up in 20 per cent of the California grapes coming on to the Canadian market.
Consumers do require more information when they are buying products. One thinks of the five million pounds of toxic pesticides that are used annually in the California grape market, which only represents those pesticides required to be registered. Canadians should be aware that this is happening and this is the intention of Bill C-222.
I like to buy Canadian produce if I have an option. Obviously, if I want to buy a mango or a papaya, the likelihood of finding a Canadian product like that is rather remote. In wintertime we enjoy eating Granny Smith apples. I would like to know whether or not they are coming from a country such as New Zealand, which I would like to support for a whole range of issues, or whether they are coming from a repressive country.
New Zealand has an admirable record on many things, particularly its anti-nuclear stand. As a consumer, I would like to use whatever impetus I have to boost its economy. If it means buying a bag of Granny Smith apples, so be it. That is my way of supporting that kind of political development in New Zealand. The intent of the bill is to be able to show support for a country as well as to boycott one. If I want to purchase produce from New Zealand, I can do that. If I want to avoid purchasing goods from Romania, I can do that as well.
This bill is very timely. I know the Committee on Justice and the Solicitor General is examining what to do with the Fruits, Vegetables and Honey Act in light of the Canada Agricultural Products Act. I urge my colleagues in the House to send a message to those people who are reviewing this legislation that the indication of country of origin is important.
I urge support of this bill for the political reasons I have outlined, so people can boycott or support certain brands of politics. I urge its support for environmental reasons, to show concern for the kind of pesticides used and concern for the health of the workers involved in the
Private Members' Business
growing of produce. This is something that is concurrent with Canadian values.
Also, regarding environmental concerns, as a world we know we are one. The degradation of agricultural land by overuse and misuse of pesticides does not only hurt the area that is involved, it hurts us all because there is a decreasing amount of arable land. The more land goes down to the devastation of agricultural degradation, the less arable land we have. In conclusion, I urge the House to support Bill C-222 so that Canadian consumers can see clearly the produce they are purchasing and where it comes from, so they can make informed judgements when they are purchasing fruit, vegetables and honey.

maintopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   FRUIT, VEGETABLES AND HONEY ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would like to say that the government believes that all Canadians should have the right to information about the food they buy, including the geographic origins of fresh produce.
The bill before us today recognizes that right and attempts to enforce it. The problem is that this legislation is not necessary. Laws and regulations requiring country of origin declarations for fresh fruits and vegetables are already in force.
Bill C-222 attempts to amend the Fruit, Vegetables and Honey Act, first passed in 1935. This bill proposes to amend that act which prohibits the sale of fruits and vegetables unless their country of origin is shown on their container or on a sign nearby.
The Fruit, Vegetables and Honey Act was amended in 1942 to prohibit imports of produce which the importer purchased later than 24 hours after shipment from the point of production. Not only did this promote a more efficient use of rail cars during the war years, but it also effectively controlled the consignment selling of fresh fruits and vegetables in this country.
When the Canada Agricultural Products Standards Act, the CAPS act, was introduced in 1955, it consolidated a number of existing acts, including the Fruit, Vegetables and Honey Act. However, the import provisions contained in regulations pertaining to consignment selling, Sections 56 and 57 as they were commonly called, were not consolidated but remained under the original act.

June 4, 1990
Private Members' Business
For over 40 years these regulations controlled imports on as consignment basis. In other words, imports could only enter Canada under a prior-purchase agreement.
However, in January 1983, the Standing Joint Committee for the Scrutiny of Regulations examined the Fruit, Vegetables and Honey Act. It ruled that the act did not have the enabling authority to regulate consignment selling.
During the following five years there was no attempt to enforce the regulations. During the summer of 1987, it quickly became apparent that Canada's fresh fruit and vegetable markets were vulnerable to surplus products from abroad. These surplus products are sold on consignment and can be sold at depressed prices, in direct competition with Canadian production and pre-pur-chased imports.
Without controls on consignment selling, produce can be imported without firm purchase agreements. Distressed or spoiled produce can enter the market, causing price disruptions in a market that is already price-sensitive.
In order to assist the Canadian horticultural industry, amendments to the CAPS act were brought before this House in June, 1988. With widespread industry support and all-party agreement, a new act, the Canada Agricultural Products Act, CAP act, received swift passage.
Statutory authority for regulations to control consignment selling of fresh fruits and vegetables was restored. Swift passage of the bill was important to the entire agri-food industry. However, it was especially crucial to Canada's horticulture sector. The Canadian Horticultural Council and the Canadian Produce Marketing Association considered the new CAP act essential to continued orderly marketing of their products.
Two years ago the remaining two sections of the fruit, vegetables and honey regulations made pursuant to the Fruit, Vegetables and Honey Act were entirely replaced by the Canadian Agricultural Products Act. The regulations were recently revoked and the Fruit, Vegetables and Honey Act is in the process of being repealed through the Miscellaneous Statute Law Amendment Program.
There are 14 different regulations made pursuant to the CAP Act. The fresh fruit and vegetable regulations
relate to the marketing of agricultural products in import, export and interprovincial trade, provide for national standards and grades of agricultural products and for their inspection and grading.
Marketing is defined in the act as, among other things, the preparation and advertising of agricultural products. Preparation in turn is defined as including processing, slaughtering, storing, inspecting, grading, packaging, assembling, pricing, marking and labelling.
Similar authority to regulate the marking and labelling of agriculture products was contained in the Canada Agricultural Products Standards Act and was the authority under which country of origin labelling requirements were written into the regulations.
The CAP Act, however, as I previously reported, replaced the CAPS Act and indicated the government's desire to regulate specifically country of origin labelling when it provided in paragraph (1) of Section 32 the authority for the Governor in Council to make regulations that provide for systems to ascertain the places of origin or destination of agricultural products.
Specifically, it is paragraph 38(1)(F) of the fresh fruit and vegetable regulations which requires a country of origin declaration on shipping containers for bulk produce, and paragraph 38(2)(B) for consumer-sized prepackaged products. The fresh fruit and vegetable regulations made under the new CAP Act prohibit the import and interprovincial trade of 29 fresh fruit and vegetables grown in Canada, if the country of origin is not declared on the packages.
We are, however, expanding this labelling requirement. Within the next few months, through a regulatory amendment to the fresh fruit and vegetables regulations, the country of origin labelling regulation will be extended to all fresh fruits and vegetables. This regulatory amendment is one of a series being processed by the government to bring about greater uniformity in the regulation of all commodities regulated under the CAP Act.
Following the final promulgation of the amendment, the country of origin regulation will apply to all types of fresh fruits and vegetables, nuts, and edible fungi. This amendment will not only bring country of origin labelling
June 4, 1990

to all these products, but it will also permit inspectors to examine, analyse and take regulatory action as required.
This will ensure that imported food products are safe, wholesome and free of contaminants for the Canadian consumer. This is something that Canadians have come to expect from their government, and we have committed ourselves to this endeavour.
In addition to the Canada Agricultural Products Act, many provincial laws regulate the sale of fresh fruits and vegetables at the retail level and call for country of origin labelling. For example, Sections 12, 13 and 14 of the Ontario Farm Products Grades and Sales Act and regulations state that there must be a declaration of country of origin on all fresh fruits and vegetables sold in bulk at the retail level. Sections 18, 19, 21 and 22 of the Quebec regulations contain the same requirements. There is also Section 7 of the Fruit and Vegetable Sales Act, Regulation 222/84 in Manitoba; Section 7 of the B.C. fruit and vegetable regulations; as well as Section 11 of the Natural Products Grades Act, Regulations 81-56, are administered by the province of New Brunswick.
We do not disagree with the idea of Bill C-222. Canadians should be informed about where their fresh produce is grown. But the fact is we do not need to amend this legislation. The right of Canadians to know is already fully protected by existing federal and provincial laws and regulations.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as assistant critic for Consumer and Corporate Affairs, I am pleased to speak on this bill, since I am extremely interested in regulations on labelling.

Bill C-222 is a Private Members' Bill to amend the Fruit, Vegetables and Honey Act of 1936. The act does not provide for the countiy of origin, something that is extremely important for Canadian consumers. The Canadian consumer is now extremely learned.

He knows what he wants, he knows his product. Canadians today are aware of chemicals, they know about pesticides and they would like to know what there is or what was used that could affect the fruit, vegetables and honey sold.
Private Members' Business
The proposal-

The bill proposes:
No person shall sell or offer for sale any produce unless the country
of origin is shown clearly and legibly on the produce or the packaging
thereof or on a sign placed near the produce.

I find this proposal very reasonable. It refers to legislation-

-a law which is soon to be repealed, the Fruit, Vegetables and Honey Act, which does not talk of the country of origin as far as labelling is concerned.
In the case of there being no grade established, there is tropical fruit, for example, which comes into the country ungraded and, therefore, unregulated.
As the member who spoke before me said, there was an act passed in 1986 called the Canada Agricultural Products Standards Act, but this particular act does not cover ungraded produce. For example, Canadian apples are regulated and graded. If apples come from outside the country, they would be similarly graded. But there is produce that comes from other countries, is not grown in Canada, and does not need to be graded. Therefore, it is not marked as to the country of origin.
I would also like to refer to the basic labelling requirements under the Food and Drugs Act and the Consumer Packaging and Labelling Act. While country of origin is required on such items as clothing, it is not required for food. Food is extremely important for the Canadian consumer. We are not any longer the consumer of the 1930s. The consumer of the 1990s is extremely literate and aware of the affects of pesticides and chemicals in food or on food. As a very literate consumer community, we want to know what is in the food, what has touched the food, and where the food comes from. It is a reasonable amendment to ask that the country of origin be included.
Perhaps the member should have added to the labelling requirements the question of meat. One million pounds of beef comes into the country in carcass or package form that is not graded. It is not marked as to the country of origin. This has resulted in the destruction

June 4, 1990
Private Members' Business
of our beef industry in Ontario, causing the closure of six packing plants last year.
I have in my hand a well-illustrated brochure put out by Canada Packers Incorporated. It shows two pictures of striploin. It states:
The striploin in picture #1 came from a carcass similar to this.
It graded Canada Grade A. To receive that Grade from the Federal Government grader, it had to meet these specifications.
a)	Youthful-Youthful carcasses mean tender meat. Notice the smooth shiny bone texture, A sure sign of youthfulness. Tenderness is the #1 quality criteria by which consumers judge your meat.
b)	A minimum fat cover of not less than 4mm and not more than 19mm-a certain amount of fat coverage is necessary to ensure good quality beef.
c)	Meat that is firm -to provide a pleasant texture for the consumer.
On the other side of this brochure it states:
The striploin in picture #2 came from a carcass similar to this-
That refers to the first picture on the front of the brochure.
Notice the porous hard texture of the bone. This animal was not youthful-the meat would look fine, but generally be tough to eat.
This cow carcass in Canada would grade D or may not be graded at all.
In the U.S. the carcass would often become "No Roll" boxed beef.
Consider these facts!
1)	There are no government quality standards for "No Roll". The packer can use whatever he wants including cows!
2)	Over one million lbs. of "No Roll" product is ending up in Canadian establishments like yours every week!
3)	Consumer studies prove that on average only one in ten unhappy customers complain to their restaurant or store, however they do tell numerous friends and associates.
I am thankful to Canada Packers for informing the consumer community. I wish that the Canadian government would respect Canadian consumers as much and publicize the differences between these meats.

So, Mr. Speaker, I note that it is necessary to indicate what country a certain product or meat comes from. I would also mention that I would even have added "meats" to the amendment.
The NDP member mentioned other reasons, political, working conditions, etc. I would simply say that we have many new Canadians here; of course, we also have many Canadians who might want to encourage buying products from some countries and maybe also discourage buying certain products, but all Canadians would have a choice if they knew the country of origin because it was indicated.
In conclusion, I sincerely and strongly support this motion to indicate the country of origin on the label of all products sold in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find it very ironic that the House is debating amendments to the bill before us. As was mentioned by the hon. member for Saanich-Gulf Islands, the justice committee is also considering the fruit, vegetables and honey act. It was referred by this House to that committee in February.
The committee is not trying to amend it. It is trying to repeal it.
The bill before us today is not necessary. As was mentioned earlier, this debate is not exactly gripping television drama. Given the problems faced by our country these days, we should be putting our time to a lot more productive use.
The fact is that the amendments found in this bill are redundant. They are already covered in the Canada Agricultural Products Act. That is why proposals have been made to repeal the Fruit, Vegetables and Honey Act through the Miscellaneous Statute Law Amendment Program.
The Miscellaneous Statute Law Amendment Program was established about 15 years ago in 1975. Since then five acts have been enacted.
This program permits minor amendments to be made to a number of federal statutes without having to wait for the particular statutes to be opened up for more substantial changes. This program is a means of correcting anomalies, inconsistencies, archaisms and errors in federal statutes. Enactments that have expired, lapsed or ceased to have effect can also be repealed through the program.
Anyone may propose amendments for possible inclusion in a set of proposals. However, most of the current proposals come from government departments or agencies.
The legislation section of the Department of Justice is responsible for receiving and reviewing proposals. As well, it prepared a document entitled "Proposals to Correct Certain Anomalies, Inconsistencies, Archaisms and Errors in the Statutes of Canada" to deal with other matters of a non-controversial and uncomplicated nature therein and to repeal certain provisions thereof that have expired or lapsed or otherwise ceased to have effect.
This document is tabled by the Minister of Justice in the House of Commons and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Solicitor General. The proposals are also tabled in the Senate and referred to its Standing Committee on Legal and Constitutional Affairs.
Consideration of the proposals by these committees has always been thorough and conducted on a non-partisan basis. I would like to emphasize that if any member
June 4, 1990

of one of the committees objects for any reason to a proposal the proposal will be dropped.
After the committees prepare their reports a miscellaneous statute law amendment bill is prepared. This bill contains only the proposals which are unanimously approved by both committees. Historically, the bills have been passed quickly, given the usual understanding that they will receive all three readings in each House without debate.
The discussion of these proposals is usually completely uncontroversial and a routine process. This is partially due to the fact that there are strict criteria for the types of proposals that the committee will consider. For example, the proposal must not be controversial, involve the spending of public funds, prejudiciously affect the rights of persons, create a new offence or subject a new class of persons to an existing offence.
Essentially, the proposals under the Miscellaneous Statute Law Amendment Act represent an attempt at legislative housekeeping. Members from all parties are in agreement with the process.
Last February when the former justice minister stood in this House to table a proposal, the member for York Centre, a member of the Official Opposition, commented on the useful nature of the process. Because I notice he is listening very intently I will quote him accurately from page 8349 of Hansard of February 15 where he is reported to have said:
I consider it a very useful device for achieving necessary changes in the laws of Canada of a non-controversial nature and also reflecting legal advice and second thoughts about certain clauses of the legislation. I have always regretted that the miscellaneous amending process is not used more openly and more generously than it is.
After that hon. member spoke, the hon. member for Burnaby-Kingsway representing the New Democratic Party stood up to agree that his party was also in favour of the proposed process. He indicated that it could be extended and used successfully to eliminate sexist language from legislation.
This year the justice committee is considering some 75 different acts that have been proposed. Up for repeal, for example, is the Trade Marks Act, overseen by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. Paragraphs 45(4)(A) to (C) of this act were excluded from the
Private Members' Business
Revised Statutes of Canada, 1985 because they deal with the renewal of the registration of trade marks that were registered under various predecessor acts of the Trade Marks Act. These paragraphs require that registration of a trade mark under the predecessor acts be renewed under the Trade Marks Act not later than July 1, 1979.
Once renewed under the Trade Marks Act, the registration of a trade mark is subject to renewal within a period of 15 years after the last renewal. As the renewal of the registration of trade marks is now governed entirely by the Trade Marks Act, there is no need to retain these transitional provisions, which are now spent.
Another statute up for repeal under the current proposals is the Fruit, Vegetables and Honey Act. This act meets all the criteria for consideration under the Miscellaneous Statute Law Amendment Program. It is not controversial. It does not involve the spending of public funds. It does not prejudicially affect the rights of persons. It does not create a new offence.
In fact, the Fruit, Vegetables and Honey Act does not do anything anymore. It has been replaced by the regulations made under the Canada Agricultural Products Act. Therefore it is not necessary to pass these amendments.

Mr. Speaker, I can assure my hon. friend that when we have been directly involved in privatization of Crown assets we have done reasonably well.
This was a subsidiary of CN which was losing some $30 million to $40 million a year. It was sold to a group of

people on the basis of the credit of the Fingold Brothers and not the individual to whom my hon. friend refers. We received $29 million for it and, as a result, the employees retained their jobs.

In its indecent haste to sell off Crown assets the government approved the giveaway of this trucking company to this man who had declared bankruptcy in 1981, a man who had defaulted on loans to four banks and one trust company and who could not even get a credit card. Latest Statistics Canada figures show that from 1986 to 1989 the Canadian dollar rose some 16 per cent against the U.S. dollar, making Canadian purchases in the United States increasingly lower in price. Do we ignore the fact that that is going to cost us jobs which will cost us business and result in a much less healthy economy? These are the questions that one has to consider when
one makes these bald, very narrow minded statements about the impact of the Canadian dollar.
It is important to understand the reasons behind the policies that the government is following. Our policies are designed to improve the health of the Canadian economy, which health has been demonstrated over the last five and a half years as Canada has been second only to Japan in economic growth in the major industrialized countries.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: NOTICES OF MOTIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I wish to raise a point of order regarding notice of a motion appearing on the Order Paper for Monday, June 4, on pages 12 and 13, under the item "Motions".
Madam Speaker, the Official Opposition maintains that the motion is erroneously listed under this item and that in doing so the government has made use of an unusual and possibly irregular procedure. I will give a short explanation, Madam Speaker, of my reasons for making this claim.
The notice of motion concerning the appointment, by the Minister of Justice, of two individuals, one as Information Commissioner and the other as Privacy Commissioner, was given, at least publicly, on June 1, last Friday. This notice of motion appears on page IV of the Order Paper under the item "Notices of Motions".
Madam Speaker, it is customary when the government tables motions for these to be transferred to government orders. I made a quick search, and I can say that although the Standing Orders were amended in 1987, if I am not mistaken, the old Standing Orders provided that when a notice of motion given by the government was called, the Chair was to transfer the motion to government orders.
Since 1987, this has happened automatically, unless- and that is the point I wish to make-the government decides to proceed by notice of motion, under the item "routine proceedings", which is now before the House. To us there is a rather considerable difference, which
June 4, 1990

may cause a number of problems. I would like the Chair to reflect on this procedure and inform me of its decision as soon as possible.
Is there a difference? Madam Speaker, I would say there is a substantial difference. Why did the government decide or insist on having these two motions for approval of the appointment of two individuals to two important positions- Why should these two appointments come under Routine Proceedings? According to us, Madam Speaker, the appointments are intended to fill two positions of officers of Parliament. The words "of Parliament" are the key words. By listing the motions under Routine Proceedings, the government approached the question as though these people were to be officers of the House. A distinction should be made between an officer of Parliament and an officer of the House.
Furthermore, Madam Speaker, I believe the government used Standing Order 67 ip), which I will read to you and which refers to motions that are called for debate.
67. (1) The following motions are debatable:
(p) such other motion, made upon Routine Proceedings, as may be required for the observance of the proprieties of the House, the maintenance of its authority, the appointment or conduct of its officers,-
The rest, Madam Speaker, is not relevant to my case.
Standing Order 67 (p) provides that the appointment of an officer of the House of Commons may be debatable. This is the argument the government is using today to bring this proposal before the House. According to us, Madam Speaker, these are not officers of the House but officers of Parliament. In other words, this House will express its position on the appointment or the proposal to appoint these two people. The Senate will also have to give its opinion. After this debate, there will be an Order in Council to appoint these two individuals. And after that, Madam Speaker, the Order in Council will come before the House for referral to and consideration by a committee, if the committee deems such is appropriate. As we know, the Standing Orders were amended some time ago, in accordance with the suggestions and proposals for parliamentary reform made by the McGrath Committee. Therefore, any order in council appoint-
Point of Order
ment is considered by committee, if the committee deems such to be appropriate.
Madam Speaker, the question before the House is quite clear. Once these appointments have been approved by the House of Commons and the Senate, once these two people have been appointed as officers of Parliament, are they responsible to Parliament or to the government? Madam Speaker, with respect, I submit that these two people are officers of the Parliament of Canada and not, strictly speaking, of the House, and certainly not of the government. My point is that they should have been transferred to Government Orders, so that the question could be debated under a quite different item.
Madam Speaker, the difference is quite substantial. I was looking at precedents, and I went back to 1983 to see what the procedure had been for appointing the two people who had occupied these positions until June 1, this year. At page 5929 of the House of Commons Journals of May 26, 1983, we find:
The following Notices of Motions, having been called, were transferred to Government Orders for consideration later this day or at the next sitting of the House,-
This was done-
- in accordance with Section 53 of Schedule II of an Act to enact the Access to Information Act and the Privacy Act, to amend the Federal Court Act and the Canada Evidence Act- this House approves the appointment of John W. Grace, Esquire, as Privacy
Commissioner.
The motion, once transferred to Government Orders, was called for debate on May 27, 1983. The debate appears at page 25796. It was initiated by the government, on motion of the hon. Mark MacGuigan-

-Mark MacGuigan, Minister of Justice, who moved then, in accordance with Section 54, that these people be named. There was a debate. The Hon. Walter Baker, the former member for Nepean-Carleton, took part in the debate, even seconded the motion. The debate was quite prolonged and interesting. Svend J. Robinson for Burnaby spoke for the NDP. The motion was adopted and we proceeded with these nominations. By order of this House, under orders of the government, that is Government Orders, a debate was held and the nominations were made.

Point of Order
Today we have a different procedure. We have under Routine Proceedings a situation where the government is treating these two positions as agents, officers, if I may use the word, of the House of Commons. They are not, Madam Speaker, I humbly submit to you, officers of the House of Commons. They are officers of Parliament.
The government has given notice under Standing Order 67(l)(p) which, in my view, is not in order. I humbly submit that we should scratch or eliminate that reference in our Routine Proceedings and also on the Order Paper and that the proper procedure be used, that the government transfer these two nominations to Government Orders as required, in my view, by the importance of the nominations, by the impact they will have, and also in my interest and this caucus' interest in our willingness to tiy to get the government to give an opportunity to Parliament to discuss all appointments, as we do today. I would like to see that done in the near future, Madam Speaker.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: NOTICES OF MOTIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it was precisely for that purpose that we proceeded in this way. The hon. House leader of the Official Opposition seems to imply some sort of conspiracy here or some attempt to bypass in some irregular way or some such notion. I suggest that he is perhaps thinking back to practices of previous governments because no such thing was intended.
The law in respect of both of these appointments requires a resolution of this House so as to make it clear that these individuals when appointed are not public servants in the same sense as being accountable to the government. The government does not have the authority under the law to direct or order those individuals. They are like the Auditor General. They account to this House for their actions and report through the appropriate committees. Yes, there is a minister who has responsibility administratively.
The Governor in Council appointment of these individuals, after resolutions of this House and the other place, is almost in the sense of a formality to give them the legal rights to collect salaries and have offices. But, in fact, these individuals are officers of this Parliament. What we sought was an appropriate means to get a resolution of this House. Standing Order 67(l)(p) states
that such motion dealing with the appointment of officers of this House is appropriate. So we moved forward under that heading to get a resolution of the House.
Why the hon. member thinks that a resolution of the House is somehow more sanctified if it comes as Government Orders, making it clear that we are talking about a government directed government decision, as opposed to having a resolution of the House under something that is not so clearly Government Orders but in fact a reflection of the House is beside me. Why he should get so worked up about it is ridiculous.
It would seem to me more appropriate to have under a provision of the House as opposed to Government Orders this motion coming forward because the individual is an officer of this House and of Parliament, not an officer of the government, not a part of government.
In Government Orders we bring forward things that the government wants to do for the benefit of the government, motions and otherwise.
This being an allotted day, I do not want to cut into the time of the opposition by proceeding with this. It seems to me a bit of a silly point since all that is being sought is compliance with the law that requires a resolution of this House and a resolution of the other place. How that resolution is done does not matter in terms of the law. This seemed an appropriate way. If it is not, there are the usual channels where we could discuss this and we need not further waste the time of the House.

speakeroldname: Mr. David Barrett (Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca) moved:
speechtext:
That a message be sent to the Senate reminding the Senate that it has the constitutional right and the power to defeat any bill coming from the House of Commons.
He said: Madam Speaker, I want to begin my comments on this very important motion by gently rereading the motion which states:
That a message be sent to the Senate reminding the Senate that it has the constitutional right and the power to defeat any bill coming from the House of Commons.
One could reasonably ask why I would sponsor such a motion, considering that in the years past and to this very moment my position on the other chamber is to abolish it. However, since no previous government has taken my advice or direction on this matter, I am now forced to debate this issue in a new context facing us in this country with a number of crises that we have on our hands.
There are three crises facing this country. One is the Meech Lake Accord, one is the free trade agreement, and last, but not least, is the infamous goods and services tax.
Earlier today we heard the Minister of Finance suggest incorrectly that Japan and Canada have the same economic performance, or relatively the same. That was part of his answer in Question Period.
June 4, 1990

I would like to refer to a report in today's edition of The Financial Post. Why am I referring to it in the context of this motion? I want it clearly understood that if there were ever a time for the Senate to prove to the Canadian people that its existence served some purpose in the context of the crisis I am going to outline in a few moments, this is the time for the Senate to kill the goods and services tax.
I want to alert my colleagues on my right in more ways than one, since they currently dominate the other place by way of appointment rather than by election. If they were serious about stopping the goods and services tax, they would not only support this motion but they would immediately call a joint caucus meeting and instruct their colleagues to block the GST in that chamber.
There are some cynics out there and some cynics in this Chamber, particularly on the government side and some of my colleagues, I must admit, who suggest that the Liberals really want the goods and services tax, that the Liberals are happy that the government brought it in, that the Liberals do not want to impede its progress, and that the Liberals want it to pass so that if and when the Liberals win the next election they will wring their hands in mock anxiety and say: 'Oh my goodness, we have inherited this terrible tax. The only way we can improve it is by bumping it from 7 per cent to 9 per cent".
Far be it for me to suggest nationally that the Liberal party would do such a thing. It would only do such a thing if it thought it would have a chance to do it. I do not suggest that the Liberal party has been absent of any sense of responsibility. Its own record does that, but I am concerned Canadian people will get the impression that the goods and services is a fait accompli when indeed we know for a fact, based on the research I did on this motion, that the Senate could stop it.
How could the Senate stop it? By a simple vote in the chamber. How could it get a majority for a simple vote in the chamber? Simple, it is a Liberal dominated other chamber. If it is temporary or not, let the government be responsible for its own actions. I know my colleagues over there are hurting because they supported this legislation and they do not like to set up someone else for a victory out of their initiative. If they were serious Liberal senators could publicly come out and say: "We
Supply
are Liberals and we are going to kill the bill". I do not think they are going to do it.
You don't?

No, and that goes back to my earlier comments about abolishing the Senate.
I believe when we really get down to it, as much as I regret to say this after my many years of public service, there is really no difference between the Liberal party and the Conservative party.
You're kidding.
No. I know that there are some differences. The most glaring difference is that one party is in and the other party is out.
Oh, oh.

I am not a very good dentist, but I will keep drilling anyway. Perhaps I have touched a nerve. I notice how quickly they respond. The fact is that they both serve the same master, only some are on the job a little while longer than the others. What has happened throughout history is that Liberals have been able to fool more people more of the time than have the Conservatives and that, no question about it, is another aspect of the difference.
Through this motion I want the Canadian people to understand if the Liberal party is truly opposed to the goods and services tax. We know where government members stand. They have decided to take the bull by the horns or whatever part of the anatomy they play with bulls with and push this bill forward. They have done it and they have used a lot of bull materials to push the legislation.
Nonetheless, the fact is that in a legislative order it is now in the other place and could be stopped there. Do you think for one moment, Madam Speaker, that a party as hypocritical and as cynical as some historians suggest the Liberal party might be would even dare to say to the public that its position is pure, decent, and honourable and that it will have the Senate kill the bill.
I have not heard Liberals say it. This is their chance. This is their time to go on record and say everything we said in committee, everything we fought against when we went to public demonstration, every speech we made on free time on CBC, and every memorandum of intent we have sent out to the voters. As we wait with bated breath for a new leader of the Liberal party, their first pro-

June 4, 1990
Supply
nouncement will be to instruct their colleagues in the Senate to stop the goods and services tax.
Voters who are seriously intending to reflect on the next election and place their support with the Liberal party, contrary to their instincts toward the Tories particularly in some areas of Ontario where it is tweedle-dee or tweedledum, should do so.
Tweedledumber.

Tweedledumber, yes. Your chance may come. Yes, that's right. Tweedledumber, your chance may come indeed.
Besides that comment why should this be done? I want to refer to a newspaper clipping which indicates that Canada's global economic standing has slipped a critical notch according to new rankings published by the International Monetary Fund on Friday and that Canada has slipped behind Italy into last place in the G-7 quota ratings. Even the Liberals who have a great deal of ability to mess things up are not capable of doing this. It also indicated that at the IMF meetings in Washington last month the brouhaha about ranking was focused on some of the other G-7 nations. The U.S., all agreed, would stay number one, but Japan's surging economic power meant that it would jump from fifth into a tie for second with West Germany in the IMF quota arrangements.
We should keep that in mind as we reflect on an answer given to a question from a colleague of mine about where Canada is in terms of the economic scale. We heard the Minister of Finance say today in the House that we were equal to Japan's growth.
Did he say that?

That is what he said, but here is what the newspaper said: "Japan's surging economic power meant that it would jump from fifth place into a tie for second. That meant that Britain and France were forced to refight another position. But a funny thing happened to the bottom line. Canada has gone to seventh place, just behind Italy".
One reason we have slipped is the goods and services tax and the inflationary impact it will have on this country.
I want to suggest that it was not just the sell-off of the CN assets that gave us this mess.
Oh, oh.

As I was about to say before I was rudely interrupted in this Chamber-and the other one has not even had the chance to interrupt-Canada's economic performance is going down. The inflationary impact of the GST by the government's own statistics is a point and a half.
Tory times are hard times.

Tory times are hard times, and Liberals only compound it. The fact is that the inflation rate will probably be more like 4 per cent or 6 per cent.
This is wreaking havoc on the poor Canadian taxpayer, the small business person, and the outside investor who wants to take a look at some rational, thoughtful, longer term investment in the country.
Canadian people expect leadership. Canadian people expect some sensitivity. The words being used on the other two crises are flexibility, thoughtfulness, compromise, and reasonableness. There is no flexibility on this one. There is no reasonableness, no compromise. It is full steam ahead into a course that is going to do more damage to this country than the other two crises.
It is extremism.

Everything is not written in stone. I would be the first one impressed if I heard the Liberal party members pledge that they will instruct their Liberal senators to block the GST and that they will insist upon it as a political party. I have not heard the Liberals do that. They are even more cynical than the Tories are. At least the Tories have taken the heat because of their ideological commitment.
Sitting over there giggling, snickering, chuckling, chortling, happy with the turn of events is the Liberal party because it knows that it can have it both ways. That is what I am trying to prevent. The Liberals are schizophrenic enough without being able to talk out of both sides of their mouth and smile in both conversations. This is a move to demonstrate-and I have the support of all the Tories in the Chamber-that politics cannot override responsibility and that the other chamber will be instructed to block the GST. I have thought about this a great deal, this one last appeal, as I reach the twilight years in my political campaign, this one last appeal to reasonableness, to sensibility, to fairness, and all I get is laughter from the Liberals.
Shame!
It hurts me to the quick.
Even your own members are laughing.

It hurts me to the quick, Madam Speaker, to have to go back to the Canadian people and tell them that they are getting fooled again by the same group that says one thing when they are in opposition, thirsting and lusting for power. They will say anything. They get back into power and laugh and giggle that they got the GST and they are going to keep it.
I am sorry that it is still early in British Columbia. I hope my grandson is in his afternoon nap. I do not want my grandson, like another generation of Canadians, to be a witness to how cynical the Liberal Party is. But, so be it, Madam Speaker, that is the case.
It is extremism.

I will conclude my comments, and I welcome questions and requests for interpretation, because I certainly will do that. Many people have asked whether there has not been enough debate about this. If
Supply
it were a simple matter, there would be no point in bringing forth this resolution. If it were a simple matter, if it is a fait accompli, there would be no point.
I want to make an appeal beyond what we have heard so far. I want to make an appeal to those people in the other chamber, should they hear my voice, or should I put it in writing that their colleagues who have subscribed to a non-elected chamber, who have packed that chamber with their political supporters, now call the chit and demand that they stop the goods and services tax.
If we see no evidence of this it will be proof positive of the thesis that I present today. It will be proof positive to every Canadian who is opposed to the goods and services tax that it is a shell game. It will be proof positive that the Liberals have only been playing games and the only real opposition to the goods and services tax is by my party, and I am proud of that.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Member for Esqui-malt-Juan de Fuca.
I would like to remind him that the New Democratic Party constitution in Article 5.2 states that the convention shall be the supreme governing body of the party and shall have authority in all matters of federal policy, program and constitution. Let me remind him of the resolution the party adopted in the federal convention in 1981 where it was stated "Be it resolved that the NDP will continue to fight for the further changes, including the abolition of the Senate".
When the hon. member was running for the leadership of his party, on December 1, 1989 in Winnipeg, a press report stated "I'm for a Triple-A Senate", said B.C. MP Ian Waddell Abolish, abolish, abolish."
Another article states: "Front-running contenders Yukon MP Audrey McLaughlin and B.C. MP Dave Barrett agreed: Abolish the Senate and use the savings to clean up the environment', said McLaughlin. 'The Senate should and must be abolished', said Barrett."
Madam Speaker, when the hon. member was a member of the legislative assembly in British Columbia, he said on December 11, 1980, in the British Columbia Hansard:

June 4, 1990
Supply
I will never give approval to appointing people to legislative bodies that have no accountability to citizens through the democratic process.
Speaking of the premier, he said: "He supports the continuation of an appointed Senate-an anachronism in this day and age of a sovereign nation. The Americans did away with it, as my colleague reminds me, in 1913. Why we have fostered and continued that hotbed of irrelevance, that hand-picked retirement bone-yard for old party hacks, and call that a Senate in terms of response to the electoral needs of the people of this country, I don't know. But when you ask me to pay tax dollars to keep that Senate going, when I've never had a chance to vote for them, then I say nay, nay, nay-never!"
What he should have said afterwards, in anticipation of this day, is, "Unless, of course, I saw some partisan advantage for the New Democratic Party". That he might have said.
I can go on at length to quote from that party but I know it is unparliamentary to use that famous word that starts with H and ends with Y and rhymes with"pocrisy". When the hon. member was talking about comparisons to Italy, he reminds me of a fellow who said, "Well, Mussolini at least got the trains to run on time". The Senate at least can kill GST. He is willing to make a pact with the devil if there was a partisan advantage. Could the hon. member stand up and tell us the difference between him and Dr. Faust?

My dear friends, may I respond to the last question first. Dr. Faust wore no clothes and, like this government, is easily exposed. If members wish for me to go on in poetry, I can think of other ways to do it. However, I am glad my friend, the hon. minister, reminded the House again of my position, which I will restate. I want the Senate abolished; the sooner, the better.
I am not in power. I hope some day, in my lifetime, that social democrats are in power. However, if it is my hon. friend's position and the Liberal Party's position to keep the Senate, then be responsible in your request if you want it to work. Is it just a burying ground for old political cronies? Is it just a place to pay off political debts, like I have always felt?
The simple answer is to prove that it has some worth and not so much for the Tories but for the Liberal Party who has consistently fought and packed the other Chamber which I oppose. They cannot have it both ways. They cannot say in this Chamber they are opposed to the goods and services tax and sit back without a Liberal Party commitment to attempt to coup it within law that exists in this country.
Madam Speaker, the Senate exists.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Do you believe in democracy?

My dear friend, if you want to elect the Senate, that is another argument. But it is not elected, it is appointed and they do have influence.
What is the philosophy of those appointees? If it is the Liberal Party philosophy, then we expect consistency. I am glad my colleague entered this debate. I am glad my colleague reminded the Canadian people of my position. My position has not changed.
If they have the legal power, and if that Party over there supports the concept, which I do not, then prove once and for all that the reason the Canadian people support the Senate is because they want to see it act and they want to see it act consistently with their position. The hon. member talks about the word beginning with H and ending with Y. You cannot have it both ways. I say we should abolish the Senate. It is there legally and I do not have the legislative authority to abolish it. You justify it and you want it, so I say to the hon. member, "Don't kid the troops".
Maybe the Tories should abolish it.
They won't. The fact is we are seeing a political game here and I do not think it is very healthy.

Madam Speaker, I hope to seek the floor to make an address myself. I am not going to be as tough on this question as was the minister from Calgary Centre, because I am willing to allow the hon. member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca to walk both sides of the street. Let him call for the abolition of the Senate and let him also call for the Senate to fulfil this remarkable role that he chooses to lay out for it.
I am glad he mentioned that he hoped his grandson was sleeping while he was making this speech and while this debate was going on. The question that went through my mind and that I wanted to address to the
June 4, 1990

hon. member when I read the resolution put forward in the hon. member's name is, "Where is Shirley"? Was Mrs. Barrett in town when the hon. member drafted this resolution? I hope this question will not be ruled out of order, but she is a sensible, intelligent woman and I am wondering whether such a mischievous and pointless resolution was put forward after some family consultation?

Madam Speaker, normally the House does not permit us to refer to spouses but in this case my colleague is correct. He knows I do consult my wife on almost everything I do, including the amount of the allowance that I get. In this case, she agrees completely. This is the only way I could word the resolution to put the Liberals on the hook. I consulted with her, we sat down, and I know that she is going to send me a bill for her consultation. I know she is going to send a sharp letter of reprimand to my good friend, maybe in Chinese. None the less, my wife and I agree the Senate should go, but as long as it is there and your parties justify it, then make it work. I suggest to the Liberal Party that it be consistent about how to make it work.
This is the closest I could come in the resolution and stay in order. They would not allow me to be any more specific at the Table. I do not blame them, they are hide-bound by 400 years of rules that do not permit clear-cut language to interfere with politics in this Chamber, so I had to explain what I could not put in writing. It is up to you Liberals. If you really mean it, tell the senators to kill the bill. I do not think you mean it; I think you have been playing politics. That is okay for a few things but not this issue. The convention is coming up. The Liberals will not bind their leader to cancel the GST, not a fig of it. My wife agrees with me on that one.

Resuming debate. The Minister of State for Finance.

Madam Speaker, thank you for the opportunity to tell you that of course I oppose this motion and also to give you the reasons why.

I think that we have just witnessed a magnificent demonstration of the NDP's great capacity for principles. The hon. member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca said that he was flexible. He has given us a very good demonstration of his flexibility and, on matters of principle, I would suggest to him that this is a bit dangerous. I could quote from him when he said, some months ago, that, "The Triple E Senate offers no hope for worthwhile changes and the Senate should and must be abolished". Therefore, it is with some dismay, I must say, that we see this motion before this House because there is here a danger to democracy.
The hon. member said he felt the need to use this motion in order to fight a measure, the GST, and that we had the economy all wrong. He quoted from an article which stated that Canada now ranks behind Italy, and so on.
It seems to me that the NDP fails to understand anything about the economy. He was referring to the quotas set up for different countries. We are very close to Italy, with a population less than one-half of that of Italy. The performance of Canada is strong and getting stronger, but the hon. member gets everything mixed up so that we do not really know where we are.

Madam Speaker, I strongly disapprove of the message that the authors of this motion are trying to put across. What is the message? Very simply, that they think it is quite all right for a non-elected unrepresentative Senate to oppose as it pleases the decisions of the elected body, the House of Commons of Canada.
We must be very clear on this. For decades, the Upper House served a very useful purpose by studying proposed legislation in advance and by sharing its concerns with us in the form of committee reports, but never interfering in the legislative process itself. Over the last several years, though, this useful non-confrontational approach

June 4, 1990
Supply
has deteriorated and we are left with a situation marked by confrontation and polarization. The motion before this House today not only endorses this unfortunate trend but seems to want to perpetuate it.
This motion must be examined in the light of the situation today and the way our parliamentary system works. For example, we must consider it taking account of what the Upper House is today, a body of appointed individuals who have no constituency and therefore no mandate from the Canadian people.
We must also consider this motion without forgetting that it was presented by a party whose goal was to abolish the other House, as we were reminded so well a few moments ago. They are not even interested in reforming the Senate. They only want to abolish it once and for all.
Finally, we must examine this motion in the light of the reasons given to justify some actions taken there. This motion seeks to support the action taken by the Upper House when it considered Bills C-21 and C-28 and the action it is threatening to take when it considers Bill C-62. It seems that polls are their only justification since they indicate that these bills are not popular with Canadians and were not part of the government's platform during the last election in 1988.

I would like to go into some detail. If we were to accept these premises, that position would make it impossible for any government to take unpopular actions.
To take a non-partisan issue as an example, I remember that members of the party opposite were strongly in favour of the abolition of capital punishment. They voted that way in the House even though the polls showed clearly that a majority of Canadians were against abolition.
Should the unelected chamber have opposed the will of the House of Commons in that case? Those opposite would have been livid at such a move because they, and many other members of the House, believed this policy was right. This motion, however, would have encouraged the Upper House to do just that, and that we cannot have.
Also, the position underlying the motion seeks to change our present parliamentary system. Representative democracy, as opposed to direct democracy, recognizes that one cannot function on the basis of daily or weekly referendums on every policy and decision. When fundamental change to the nature of a country is at stake, or when society is equally divided on an issue, then direct reference to the people may be necessary. But the basis of our system of government is that governments are judged at elections, on the basis of their past actions and their proposed policies. If the people do not like what they see, then they will elect another party to power.
By supporting the actions of the unelected second Chamber, on the basis that specific policies are unpopular, this motion seeks to bootleg into our system of government what amounts to a system of referendums. If those opposite want to change the system, then that is their privilege. But they should do so openly and clearly, and in a fashion that permits a debate on that particular subject to take place. They should not be trying to change our system of government in this way.
Finally, in terms of the context in which this motion is being put, I want to consider the moral authority behind these policies. After all, the basis for the actions the other place has been taking, or is threatening to take, is that the people do not want them because of what polls tell them. Our system of government relies on the concept that platforms are presented at general elections and that the people judge those programs. I have heard it argued that the policies in these bills were not before the people in 1988 and therefore it is legitimate to hold them up.
In fact, these policies-not in their details but in their principles-were an integral part of the policies before the people in 1988. They are firmly based in the economic actions we took from 1984 to 1988. They respond clearly to concerns we have had since 1984 and which were before the people in 1988.1 cannot accept that the results of the election of 1988 had nothing to do with our economic record and our approach to economic issues.
As I have said, there are three specific pieces of legislation at issue right now. In concrete terms they are what this debate is about. Their measures respond to urgent needs. They were developed as part of an over-all
June 4, 1990

economic strategy we have been following since 1984, and which has already met with some success in strengthening and energizing the economy.
Let me look briefly at each of these bills from the viewpoint of economic policy.
Bill C-21 carries out badly needed reforms in our system of unemployment insurance. The system we inherited in 1984 was in desperate need of changes-everybody admitted that. We proceeded carefully and on the basis of consultation. In Bill C-21 we proposed a set of changes to the system which makes it more flexible and more responsive to the concerns of those who really need it.
At the same time we were able to redirect some of the resources in the system to enhance the role of retraining and education. Part of our economic reality is that there is a need for people to gain new skills and to get better training. That is the key to higher employment and greater prosperity. By delaying the legislation as it has done, many individuals have been deprived of benefits and opportunities to which we believe they are entitled.
Bill C-28 implements the Income Tax Act related amendments from the 1989 budget. I want to recall that one of the greatest economic challenges we face is inflation. The damage it does to the economy and to individuals is something we experienced in the early 1980s. We do not want to go through that again.
Since 1984 our government has been engaged in a battle with inflationary pressures. One important way in which we have done this is by working to lower the deficit fairly and acceptably. Right now, as a result of the size of the debt and the deficit we inherited, as well as the effects of compounding interest on the debt, 35 cents of every revenue dollar must be spent on paying that interest.
Limiting government spending and increasing revenues are the two ways in which the deficit can be brought down. We have moved on both fronts. The measures in Bill C-28 are part of our over-all policy to fight the deficit in as fair a way as possible. This policy has met with some success. We have moved from the 1984 situation, where spending on programs exceeded revenues by $16 billion, to the situation outlined in the February budget, where revenues exceeded program

spending by $10 billion last year. If we are to build on this progress, however, we must continue the battle. By delaying the implementation of the measures in Bill C-28, the other Chamber is harming and not helping this effort.
The third piece of legislation in question is Bill C-62, which implements the goods and services tax. I want to remind all hon. members that this is not a proposal suddenly produced out of the blue in 1989. Tax reform was urgently needed by the economy, and our government's concern about this has been known from the beginning of our term of office. Initially, we proceeded by closing loopholes and administrative reform, while a larger reform of the system was studied. We proceeded with stage one of that reform after a great deal of consultation before the 1988 election. We have continued to work toward a better system of taxation for Canada.

We have also made it clear from the start that the manufacturers' sales tax reform was an integral part of our tax reform. The flaws of that antiquated tax were pointed out time and time again. They have been disclosed on many occasions both within and outside this House. We indicated clearly that the second stage in this tax reform would involve the transition to a different system, with as wide a base as possible. Once those provisions were made public, we stayed tuned into the public and made a number of changes based on the needs that were expressed to us.
The principles that were going to be used were laid out in the Budget in 1987 and 1988. This motion seeks to encourage the other place to withold, amend, or, better still, reject the provisions of Bill C-62 without any regard for the principles of electoral democracy. It jeopardizes the economy of this country.
I would also like to ask those who support this motion to tell me where all this will lead us? We have three bills in abeyance. All are very important for the economy as well as for the well-being of Canadians. All are an integral part of the economthe elected govemement of this country. Still, if that motion were to be taken seriously-there are times when one wonders-all bills passed in this House, even uninanimously, would be dealt with the same way. We would convert to a system where the legislators elected by the people would systematically clash with a body of non elected individuals

that does not have a comparable moral authority and does not have to account for its actions.

The motion therefore seeks to undermine the principle underlying our system of elections and responsible government. It ignores the fact that the measures which they oppose were part of the election platform of the government in 1988, and that this government won re-election on the basis of that platform.
I stand in favour of the elected House and its historic rights. I stand in favour of the government elected by the people of Canada. I stand in favour of the economic policy presented to the people in two successive general elections and approved by them.

On the other hand, Madam Speaker, I must say in concluding that I object to what the non-elected members of the upper House have been doing and to the role they have given themselves. They should never have taken on such a role, which they had never sought to play until these past few years. I object to them claiming a moral authority equivalent to that of this House. Finally, I oppose this motion whose purpose is to legitimize their actions and alter the very nature of our system of government.

Madam Speaker, in principle, we must always take seriously the resolutions that are presented and debated in this House. With this in mind, I would like to discuss the resolution proposed by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca. Since it is very short, I would like to start by reading it:
That a message be sent to the Senate reminding the Senate that it
has the constitutional right and the power to defeat any bill coming
from the House of Commons.
But, Madam Speaker, with all due respect for the Order Paper and resolutions, I stress that this resolution is not to be taken seriously, as I believe our New Democratic colleague himself admitted.

This resolution is a piece of mischief which is designed as a matter of NDP strategy to make it look as if the Official Opposition, of which I am very proud to be a member, is in favour of the free trade agreement and the goods and services tax.
You have to go a long way to try to make an argument like that. I want to suggest that the resolution that has been put before us just does not do it. It is not a resolution that can be taken seriously in any sense of the word.
It is ironic that a joke should be put on the Order Paper of the House of Commons at a time when there are so many serious things to discuss about the Senate and about the relationship between the Senate and the House of Commons.
We are sitting in this House doing our work, knowing that the more momentous events of today for the future of our country are taking place across the street. They are in the hands of the duly elected representatives of the legislatures of the provinces of our country, and of our national government, who is not a Liberal but a Progressive Conservative, who are working across the street to try to find a solution to the constitutional impasse that faces us. That is where the important things are happening today.
But if there is going to be light at the end of the tunnel, it is bizarre and ridiculous, and I am not going to put it any higher than that, for the New Democratic Party to take today to tell us that the Senate should be abolished and to remind senators that they have the constitutional right and power to defeat any bill coming from the House of Commons. What does that have to do with anything?
What I want to reflect on today in these brief remarks is what we should be saying about the Senate, what we should be asking about the Senate. Starting from a very simple first principle-

An item of these discussions, as we are led to believe, is the Senate. It is hardly the time to come up with these kinds of ridiculous discussions.

However, I think we should discuss these problems where they have to be discussed.
What I do not like about this motion is that it would give the appearance of support from an elected House, which is this House, to powers that we do not recognize in the Senate. The tradition, which is very important in our British parliamentary system, has to do with what the powers of the Senate are. We have seen them over the years, and we may not like them. Madam Speaker, I will spare the House a repetition of the brilliant remarks with which I opened my intervention. I would like simply to pick up on the question asked by the NDP member who rose to ask the minister a question. He asked him to admit that under
