our Constitution the Senate has the power, as the motion states, to defeat any bill coming from the House of Commons. The answer to that question is, yes, the Constitution does give that power to the Senate.
But that is not the end of the issue, as the minister pointed out. Unfortunately, to the NDP that does seem to be the end of the issue. Let me tell him and the other members of the NDP that our Constitution needs to be updated. It needs to be updated in more ways than one and in more places than one. If he would care to pay some attention to the national debate that is going on in the country, nowhere is there more dissatisfaction than there is with the place of the Senate in the Constitution of Canada. We want to do something about that.
As I mentioned, while we are sitting here, the constitutional impasse which is labelled "Meech Lake" may be working itself out. If I can give some more news to the NDP, one of the great benefits is that then we may be able to do something to reform the Senate. We may be able to make out of it an institution which a democracy will recognize as having a legitimate function that it can exercise.
It is in an awkward situation now because, unlike a lot of anachronisms, this anachronism is a living organism. It is an organ of Parliament. It is composed of well-meaning Canadian citizens determined to do their duty for their country, hidebound somewhat by the inappropriate amount of power that is awarded to them under this anachronistic and hopefully soon to be revised constitutional aspect of Canada.
I have had the pleasure of being a member of Parliament during the time when our party was in power and in control of the Senate by having a majority of members of the Senate also of our party. I have also served in this period when we are in the Opposition in this party but in the majority in the Upper House.
That exercise of constitutional rights of the Senate, under those circumstances, in eveiy case and on a wall to wall basis of agreement with what the Opposition in the Lower House would like would defy a basic requirement of a democracy.
I do not like to admit it with members of the Conservative party present in the room, but the Liberals were defeated in the last election. I see nods of agreement. We were defeated in the election of 1984. It is very important that that be recognized in the way that Parliament operates.
Members of the NDP say that the Liberal party, in spite of having been defeated in 1984 and in 1988, has this anachronistic, constitutional power to defeat any bill coming from the House of Commons, and that we should do it or else we are not being true to our principles. Our basic principle is democracy. We have to accept the will of the people.
Like with the UI bill in the Senate right now?

I want to make two more brief points and then I will be very happy to have questions from my hon. friend.
My first point is how can we operate in those circumstances where the majority of members are Liberals, where they do not agree with the GST, the free trade agreement, or with a government which is trying more and more to eliminate the middle class and to divide Canadians into a two-Canada idea of a rich powerful centre tied very closely to the United States to the exclusion of the rest of the world and the regions of the country which are to be, in its way of looking at it, a source of population flows into the greater populated areas of our country. That is its vision. It is proud of it. It has people in the country who support it and who help it to achieve those objectives. We do not. It is not for the Senate, although controlled by a majority of Liberal members, to contradict the result of the last election.
I did not vote Conservative in 1984 and I did not vote Conservative in 1988. But, enough Canadians did vote Conservative to put this House under the authority of that party. In the Senate, where there are a majority of Liberal members, I think they have been very creative, very respectful of the democracy which is Canada, and I think they have achieved a lot. They have spoken as an Upper House in a federal system should for those who are not fairly represented by the basic application of one person, one vote. They have spoken for depopulating regions of our country where industries are being pulled out by the government, or are being pulled out by the operation of the so-called free market established under the free trade agreement. They have spoken for the

francophone minorities in parts of the country where they do not represent enough of a population to have a real democratic voice. They have spoken for cultural minorities. They have spoken for aboriginal people. They have spoken for the poor. They have spoken for religious minorities within the country. And in each case they have not said, as it states in the resolution "We have the power to defeat any bill coming from the House of Commons and we intend to do it". They have said "Look again at what you are trying to do". They have said to Canadians "Look again at what this destructive government is trying to do to our beloved country". That has been the role of the Senate under present arrangements.
If there is light at the end of the Meech Lake tunnel, the light is that we can develop and I am confident that we can do it. I hear so many talk about the obstacles and the vested interests. I do not believe it. I believe there is a great will in this country to have a Senate that will work for us.
A lot of people believe that Ontario and Quebec will never relinquish their control of the Senate in terms of the numbers of seats they have in relation to the other regions of our country. Madam Speaker, I know it is not news for you, but I think it is news for a lot of Canadians to know that that is just not true.
The number of seats from Ontario and Quebec do not constitute a majority of the number of seats in the Senate. They constitute less than a majority and, speaking as a member from Ontario who has watched the Senate over the years, I cannot remember when it was significant in any of our decisions that the Ontario delegation was more substantial than the delegation from two or three other provinces put together. That is not the way the Senate was inclined to operate.
I want to talk for a moment about some of the evidence that did not get the attention that it should have, that was brought before the committee chaired by the hon. member for Sherbrooke on which I had the great honour to serve, about some of the interesting features of the Senate. Ontario now has 24 seats. If you go by population, it should have 37.1 would like to say, if I may interject, that this is evidence given by a lawyer from Winnipeg, Patrick Riley. When we are looking at what will follow Meech Lake, we should be looking at things like this. We should not be looking at the historic and anachronistic fact that in 1867 a deal was made on the establishment of the Senate which, even then, was the most controversial issue in the formation of Canada. There were more arguments about how the Senate should be formed and what delegations should come from each province than there were about almost any other issue, including the place of minority language rights in our country.
We have been complaining about our Senate for 120 years. Here is a member standing up, wanting us to pull the trigger that the Constitution gave us 120 years ago, over the democracy which we have built by having senators who have been restrained, discreet, intelligent and effective when they have chosen to speak up for interests that this government has cared so little for and has done so much to abuse.
I know this motion is not coming to a vote. I am hoping, as much as a patriotic Canadian can hope, that the serious issue of Senate reform is soon before us because it will mean that we are moving ahead in building our country not moving backward, as the NDP wants to suggest for a cheap political shot.

Madam Speaker, at the outset, let me say it is my intention to speak only for 10 minutes, perhaps less. I am sure that will come as a source of considerable joy to the members here today. My colleague from Okanagan-Shuswap may also get in on the debate. I consider it, let's say, an indulgence in the desires of the Elouse.
I would like to say at the outset that like my hon. colleague, the member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca, I too will attempt to avoid the use of the h word. It is not going to be easy but I want you to know that I am going to do my best to avoid that word in addressing what is in fact the nub of the matter before us today. That is, can the Canadian people trust the Liberal party to put their Senate majority where their mouth is. That is the only question before the House today, although for the purpose of the observance of the parliamentary niceties, it was necessary to draft the motion in a somewhat less straightforward fashion.
I would like to suggest that the Canadian people are finding out that no, they cannot trust the Liberals where they have the ability to abolish the GST to do so. They

can trust the Liberals to rail against it impotently in the House of Commons but they cannot trust the Liberals to use their Senate majority to defeat the GST in the other place. We know that for a fact because of May 3. May 3 was the day on which the other place passed the GST bill at second reading. That was the day on which the Senate, in which the majority of members are Liberals, approved in principle the GST. That is something that all Canadians should remember.
There were headlines in The Toronto Star.

I wish that were the case. I wish I could have surreptitiously sneaked into the House this afternoon and could have stood here and held up, although I know it is against the rules of the House, a copy of The Toronto Star with a 96-point headline on the front page stating: "Senate Liberal Majority Approves GST". It grieves me deeply that I am unable to do that because to the best of my knowledge no such 96-point headline was ever featured in The Toronto Star.
Why that is, of course, must remain a matter of speculation. What must not remain a matter of speculation, however, is the performance of the Liberals in the Senate. They had the chance on May 3 to defeat the GST and let it slip by quietly, rather like a weasel nosing around the chicken coop at night.
There are some in this Chamber who believe that the New Democratic Party seeking the action of the Liberals in the Senate to defeat the GST somehow constitutes an abandonment of the party's principled opposition to the Senate. I would like to assure the House of two things. First, the NDP is in no way lessened in its absolute and fundamental opposition to that other unelected, undemocratic-I must stop myself before I get into territory of perhaps unparliamentary adjectives, Madam Speaker, suffice to say that the NDP remains absolutely opposed to the current other place and given a day's chance would abolish it.
What comes after? What form might some subsequent second house in this Parliament take? That is a matter for legitimate debate. I can tell you, Madam Speaker, as I believe to be the case in other caucuses in this House. In the NDP caucus there is a wide variety of opinion as to what form some future second chamber might take. There is no wavering in our caucus in its absolute

opposition to the current nonsense that we call the Senate.
People are having trouble this afternoon getting around the fact that we can both favour the abolition of the current Senate, acknowledge that it is there, and call upon it to do something the overwhelming majority of Canadians want done.
I would remind the Liberals that when they held up the free trade agreement in 1988, they did so when public opinion polls showed, roughly, on a good day that 50 per cent of Canadians were in clear opposition to the deal.
I have not seen a poll of Canadian public opinion with regard to the unemployment insurance bill. My guess is, as sad as it is to have to admit it, that the majority of Canadians are unaware of that bill now before the Senate. Yet it is being made the subject of rigorous action by the Liberal majority in the Senate.
With the GST we have a tax initiative by the Conservative government that is opposed by up to 80 per cent of Canadians. In the last poll I saw a clear majority, in excess of 50 per cent, wants it defeated in the Senate. It does not trouble them.
In an attempt to clarify the question of how one can both favour the abolition of the Senate and at the same time favour the current Senate's destruction of the GST, I would like to give the House a little analogy. I am hoping this will make it a little easier to understand.
Let us say you just bought yourself a house. It is a nice old house. It has clapboard siding, solid hardwood floors, high ceilings, and a big backyard. It is a beautiful place, but in the middle of that big backyard is the largest damn crab apple tree you ever saw in your life. You have nothing against crab apple trees, Madam Speaker. The little old couple next door when you were a kid used to give your parents delicious crab apple jelly every fall. There is lots of fun to be had in climbing big, old crab apple trees.
However, the trouble with this crab apple tree is that it is so huge and so obstructive that nothing much can grow in the backyard. It shades virtually the entire area, making a vegetable garden impossible, and its root system sucks virtually all the water and nutrients out of the soil so that not even a lawn can grow well.
As much as you do not mind crab apples, you resolve to tear this tree down. You want to put in a vegetable garden. You want a nice lawn. Having decided that you are going to get rid of the big, old crab apple tree as soon as you can get the money and time together to do so, are you being somehow dishonest, unprincipled or two-faced if you take advantage of the crab apple tree in the meantime?
Are you going to ignore the crab apples that the tree produces and just let them rot on the ground, or are you going to eat a few and maybe tty your own hand at making some crab apple jelly? Are you going to tell your kids: "No, no, you cannot play in that big, old tree because some day we are going to get rid of it."? Are you going to refuse to seek shelter in its shade on blistering hot days? Of course not. That would be dumb as a bag of hammers.
In doing any of those things you are in no way abandoning your long-term goal of tearing down the tree and replacing it with a nice vegetable garden and a lawn. "Aha," some may say, "but what if in using the crab apple tree as it stands you get to like it or even cherish it so that finally all thought of tearing it down disappears," to which sensibly, Madam Speaker, you would reply: "Sure, I might like it, but I know I will like having that vegetable garden and that nice lawn a whole lot more. If I really got to like having a crab apple tree around, hell, I will plant a new one, but it will be smaller and in a different location."
It is just so with the Senate. The fact is that it is there. We can ignore it, but that will not make it go away. We can offer our perfectly reasonable and long overdue arguments to the effect that, in its present form at least, it ought to be abolished, but at present we do not have the power necessary to effect that policy. In the meantime it is there. In fact it does not matter a tinker's damn what we think of the Senate. It is there.
The only question is: It being there, will we call upon it to do the right thing for the people of Canada, an overwhelming majority of whom have identified a clear wish regarding the GST? Or, will we confuse principle with wishful thinking and try to pretend that the damn tree is not even there?
The alternative to myself and my colleagues in the NDP is clear. Again let me state and close with the obvious. The Liberals have a majority in the Senate. They can use that majority to axe the tax, to kill the bill, to get rid of the GST. Their failure to do so-I predict that it will be a failure to do so-can only in future be

seen by Canadians as a clear statement by the Liberal party that they favour the GST.

In other words, on May 31, two or three days ago, the New Democrats wanted to take all the money away from the Senate. Today they are telling Canadians that they want to tell the Senate to defeat the bill.
Where do members of the NDP stand? I know they do not have much of a stand on anything. We always think they are either coming or going somewhere, but are they for the Senate, for the Senate's money or not? If they are not for it, okay. If they are for no budget, how can you operate without any money? If they are not for having a budget how can we have this motion today, which would be consistent? How about some consistency in the debate for a while?

Madam Speaker, I am indebted to the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier for raising that most cogent and praiseworthy motion by our hon. House leader to abolish the budget of the Senate. It is utterly consistent with the policy of the New Democratic Party which is to abolish the other place as currently it stands. I do not want anybody in this House to harbour any doubts in this regard. The NDP unequivocally favours the abolition of the current Senate, without any exception or reservation whatsoever.
In this as in so much else we have, it must be admitted, experienced a wee bit of difficulty in convincing the rest of you of the wisdom of this position, the case in point being the fate of that very motion at the end of May. We
Supply
are left trudging along with this sclerotic, nonsensical other place for the time being. That being the case, let me say again that the point of the motion has much less to do with the Senate and much more to do with the Liberal party. As I said at the beginning, what it boils down to is: Will the Liberal party or will the Liberal party not put its Senate majority where its mouth is?

Madam Speaker, I would just like to read some quotes to show the elasticity of the NDP's position. The hon. member for Edmonton East says that it is utterly consistent and absolutely in favour of abolition. I would like to refer to an magazine article in the Alberta Report magazine which reads:
Many in the western wing of the NDP recognize there is widespread popular support in their region for an elected, equal and effective Senate. And Saskatchewan NDP leader Roy Romanow now concedes there is an alternative to abolition.
That is how utterly consistent they are. It goes on to say:
Mr. Romanow, among the four western NDP leaders, seems most willing to consider some kind of Senate reform as an alternative to abolition. But the others appear willing to listen, at least. "I am open to ideas on (Senate reform)", says Mr. Doer.
There are two NDP leaders in the west who are not in favour of abolition but in favour of reform. It goes on to say:
- Mr. Waddell professes to be a Senate abolitionist, but he too concedes that reform is worth considering. Some NDPers are coming to accept that it looks like the Senate is going to be around for a while longer, so we might as well have one that does something.
And it concludes by saying:
Mr. Romanow clearly understands these political realities as well or better than most. "Let's face it", he says, "I've been in politics in Saskatchewan for a long time, and the name of the game is more of a voice for the West".
I would like to have the hon. member respond to these utterly consistent remarks that the NDP has made on this situation.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It will have to be a short rebuttal from the hon. member for Edmonton East.

Madam Speaker, as I was to the previous Liberal speaker, I am indebted to this one for raising the obvious fact. I will repeat it, and I hope it sticks this time. The NDP is absolutely, utterly, without exception, consistent in favouring the abolition of the current Senate. What is to replace it? That is a

June 4, 1990
Supply
matter of debate in our caucus, as in yours, and as in theirs, but the question of the current Senate in its current form, no.

Madam Speaker, I would just like to read the motion to get us back on track:
That a message be sent to the Senate reminding the Senate that it
has the constitutional right and the power to defeat any bill coming
from the House of Commons.
There are many divergent opinions in terms of the relevance or irrelevance of the Senate and the future of that body. That argument, itself, is irrelevant to this currrent debate. The fact is that we do have a duly constituted body with certain legislative authorities, and we are calling on that body to exericse those legislative authorities.
Canadians throughout this country I think honestly believe that the GST is now essentially a fait accompli and that they have no more room to manoeuvre, to debate, or to discuss. The fact is that the GST still can be stopped.
The Senate is currently studying this legislation. Not all Canadians realize that the Senate has the capacity not only to recommend changes, not only to study the bill, but to kill the legislation, to stop it DOA. The Senate has a legitimate role in our parliamentary system and this is one aspect of that legitimate role.
I submit to you, Madam Speaker, that it is a role that has become increasingly relevant because of the very unparliamentary jackboot tactics that have been used by this government in ramming some of the legislative initiatives down the throats of ordinary Canadians. It has used closure well over a dozen times in only the last legislative sitting.
Peter Hogg has written in The Constitutional Law of Canada, 1985 that the Constitution Act, 1867, gives to the Senate the same powers as the House of Commons except that money bills must originate in the House of Commons.
Essentially, the Senate has the same legislative authority as has the House of Commons. One might ask if the Senate ever before defeated legislation from the House of Commons? In 1920 the Senate rejected measures that were forwarded to it by a minority Liberal
government. Between 1925 and 1930 no fewer than 48 bills were amended by the Senate and 12 bills were rejected. In the 1930s five bills were defeated by the Senate.
So legal precedents have been established which ascertain the Senate's authority and capacity to deep six bad legislation. The Senate has a responsibility to act. It has established that responsibility and it should exercise that responsibility.
Why do my colleagues and I call for Senate action? The fact is that this government has used every opportunity available to it to shut down the democratic process, to deep six any real debate going on in this country about the goods and services tax. It has used closure time and time again and has essentially disenfranchised opposition members of Parliament from carrying out their duties in bringing forward the concerns of their constituents.
And illegal closure in committee.

As my colleague from Esquimalt- Juan de Fuca adds, illegal closure at the committee stage of the GST legislation.
This is why we are asking the Senate to exercise its due authority. We are asking the Senate to kill the bill and that request is not at odds with any perception of whether the Senate should be reformed or abolished. That argument is irrelevant. We are asking it to do the job that it has authority to do right now.
We have called for the Senate to study the bill. To allow it to study the bill and do nothing about it would be hypocritical. If you are going to give the Senators the bill to study, you have to give them the authority to defeat the bill if they so desire. Asking the Senate to defeat the bill could, certainly, provoke a constitutional crisis. Well, so be it. That constitutional crisis may hopefully provide some initiative for real Senate reform.
The Liberals want to rag the puck on this one, make no mistake about it. Have a look at the numbers. The Liberals now dominate the Senate with 54 seats. The Conservatives have 33 seats, there are four independents, 1 independent Conservative and 12 vacancies. The Liberals are just trying to rag the puck until this Tory government comes in and stacks the deck so it can ram through the GST legislation and the Liberals can stand back and say: "Gosh we tried to defeat it but those nasty Tories went and stacked the deck against us. How could we defeat the legislation when that nasty Tory govern-
June 4, 1990

ment came in and stacked the deck by appointing new Tory Senators? We could only do what we could."
The Liberals want to see this legislation passed. Their leadership candidates have been strangely quiet on this. They have been rubbing their hands in glee just waiting for the Tories to come in and stack the deck in the Senate so that they can ram it through. They want to let the Tories take it on the chin for bringing in the GST and likely go down the tubes as a result of it, then they can sit back and become the beneficiaries.
I have criticized this government many times, but at least it deserves credit for sticking to its ideology. The Liberals have had no ideology on this except the raw pursuit of power. They have been laying in the weeds on this one. They have been praying that the GST comes through and that they can capitalize on it in the long run. The Liberals should not be allowed to fool the Canadian people.
This Liberal dominated Senate has a duty to the people of Canada, and that is to kill the bill now. The people should be encouraged to write their Senators, to write the Liberal leader and urge the Senate to block this GST legislation. Better yet, perhaps the people of Canada should call the toll free number to the Senate: 1-800-267-7362.
What was that number again?
1-800-267-7362. Anybody in Canada can call that number.
I am sorry, I didn't quite get that.
My colleague asks for the number again. It is 1-800-267-7362. Pick up the phone, dial the number, tell the Senate to kill the bill.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Questions or comments? The hon. member for Scarborough-Rouge River.

Madam Speaker, my colleague with the New Democratic Party is surely trying to sell water beds to the House of Commons. The motion placed before the house is also-I do not want to use the word "misleading"-but I think doing a disservice to the Senate. The Senate is there to refine, review and modify legislation that has been passed by the House of Commons. It is not there to kill
Supply
anything. It never was there to kill anything. My friend in the New Democratic Party does a disservice to the Senate by suggesting that its role is to kill anything that has been created by us in this House of Commons.
I would like him to square what they are really after here with the reality of the function in the Senate. If there were, by happenstance, a member of the Senate here in the gallery of this chamber watching, he or she would be aghast at the perception of the Senate perpetrated by the member representing the New Democratic Party here. I think that is very unfair to the Senate. The knowledge of the Senate by those on that side of the House is perhaps too sophisticated by half. Their ignorance is showing through here this afternoon.
Would the member offer the Senate something constructive that is in keeping with the Senate's own function?

Madam Speaker, when legislation is debated fully in any parliamentary procedure it is not done with the threat of closure used not once, not twice but over a dozen times. It is not done with the threat and, in fact, the sanction of illegal closure at the committee stage of legislation, as was the case with this legislation.
We are saying that because this government has abrogated the responsibilities of this chamber by the illegal use of unparliamentary procedures, it has in fact disenfranchised the vote of every Canadian taxpayer out there. Because of that we are saying that the Senate has at this point become the locus of democratic dissent in this country. The Senate should carry out its responsibilities because of the fact that this government has not allowed full democratic participation. Use the Senate to kill the bill.

Madam Speaker, does the member truly believe that if the Liberal Party wanted to kill the GST it could kill it in the Senate? Are there precedents for this? Could they not be instructed, as Liberal appointees, to do what they say they want done? In light of the fact that they acknowledged in this House in the earlier debate that closure was the wrong thing to use in committee, that closure was the wrong thing to use in the House, is it not logical that they would follow through? Give the members one or two precedents to ease their conscience.

Supply

Madam Speaker, my colleague for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca has waxed eloquent once again in terms of the real essence of the issue. Precedence was established many years ago for using the Senate to kill bad legislation that has been brought to the other Chamber by the House of Commons. As I indicated earlier, from 1925 to 1930 the Senate rejected 12 pieces of legislation. During the 1930s no fewer than five bills were defeated by the Senate Chamber.
I say to you, Madam Speaker, and to my colleague, that legal precedence for the Senate's authority and capacity to deep six legislation has been well established.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The time for questions and comments has now expired. Resuming debate, the hon. member for Jonquiere.

Madam Speaker, I rise in the House today to respond to and comment on the motion of the hon. member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca which says the following, and I quote:
That a message be sent to the Senate reminding the Senate that it
has the constitutional right and the power to defeat any bill coming
from the House of Commons.
Madam Speaker, first of all I must say it is passing strange that a representative of a party that has constantly demanded the abolition of the Senate in its present form should move a motion supporting the constitutional right and power of the Senate to shoot down a bill coming from the House of Commons.
It should come as no surprise that I wondered whether we should take this motion seriously. Especially, Madam Speaker, when we consider that at this very moment, eleven First Ministers are meeting a few streets down to try and resolve the constitutional impasse and save a country that is on the verge of breaking up. One of the strategies of the 11 First Ministers is to reform a Senate that no longer meets the demands and needs of the day. In fact, all members of this House know perfectly well we must proceed with a number of changes.
However, I had only a brief moment's hesitation, since the motion of the member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca is certainly an opportunity to discuss a number of very interesting constitutional issues which may have eluded the understanding of the hon. member for the New Democratic Party. It would be a big mistake to hesitate, and it will be interesting, Madam Speaker, to see how the Liberals in the House will vote when the question is put on the motion.
Madam Speaker, like all our activities in the House, this is a proposal that should be approached with the same care as any other measure that concerns the proper operations of government. My concerns in considering the motion are above all practical, especially with respect to C-21 which is now being held up in the Senate. I know perfectly well that the purpose of this motion, Madam Speaker, was to deal directly with C-21, the bill on unemployment insurance reform which has now been shuttling between the Senate and the House of Commons for several months, although we all know the bill should have come into force on January 1 this year.
It is obvious that there has been sufficient debate on the constitutional rights and powers of the Senate. In fact, some people might even wonder why we are talking about this.
All partisanship aside, Madam Speaker, does anybody in this House seriously believe that our responsibility to the people of Canada must be undermined by a non-elected and non-answerable assembly? Yet this protracted exercise has been going on for months, has drawn the attention of Canadians from coast to coast, and even forced the Speaker of the Commons to make a ruling.
Our Speaker's judicious admonitions notwithstanding, the game is still going on and our parliamentaiy system is paralyzed. Democratic precedents, public opinion, common sense, in short everything seems to indicate that the Senate cannot block government legislation, especially when it has an impact on public expenditures.
But it has become obvious that we are in a situation which simply does not relate to democratic principles nor even common sense. For the past few years we have been up against systematic abuse of power on the part of the Liberals.
June 4, 1990

Today's motion is the latest example of the incoherence and opportunism which have been the highlights of the debate. I say incoherence because even such Liberals as Senators MacEachen and Frith once stated that the Senate should yield to the House of Commons, thus acknowledging a parliamentary principle established some 80 years ago.
I would not want to create the impression that the Senate does not have a role to play, but I am sure a distinction must be made between constructive criticism about bills and the weakening of the fundamental rights of the elected House of Commons. The Speaker drew attention to that fact when referring to the important powers the Senate would take away from the elected Lower House.
In his ruling of April 26 last the Speaker recalled a number of precedents in that respect. The non-elected Senate simply does not have a mandate to thwart the adoption of bills to allocate public funds. To tiy to have such a motion passed is potentially disastrous not only administratively but for the Canadian people and for our democracy as well.
In spite of the attempts made by the Minister of Employment and Immigration so that the concerns of the Senate be taken into account in the bill, the Liberal senators keep interfering with the business of this elected House. The dead-end created by such tactic has serious implications for the Canadian workers across the country.
As the hon. members know, Madam Speaker, Bill C-21 is an integral part of the Labour Force Development Strategy based on the establishment of partnerships with the private sector to maintain a training tradition in Canada and to promote the betterment of our human resources skills. As long as Bill C-21 has not been passed, such urgent business will in large part be left in mid air.
In times of technological evolution and increased international competition, Canada can not afford to delay even very slighly the implementation of the Labour Force Development Strategy and other initiatives related to human resources planning.
To delay a bill providing for additional unemployment benefits and training resources may be of no consequence for the Liberal senators, but things are quite different for millions of Canadians.
Supply
I should like to point out to you, Madam Speaker, that the members of the Senate are paid every week, their salary is garanteed, and that they do not have to account to the public for anything since they have been appointed for life, while the members of this House must face the public every four years and account for their decisions. That gives you an idea of the difference between us, who must make decisions while taking the Canadians into consideration, and that other group of individuals who is not accountable to the people.
To give you an idea of the implications of the Senate's conduct as well as to show clearly what this motion seeks to do, allow me, Madam Speaker, to take a moment to set some elements of Bill C-21 in the context of the Labour Force Development Strategy.
Madam Speaker, I am talking about Bill C-21 since I travelled across Canada with several of my colleagues to hear what Canadians thought about it.
If Bill C-21 is passed, the government will be able to implement substantially extended human resources planning programs in co-operation with industries throughout the country.
If Bill C-21 passes, the funds available would allow us to launch employment equity initiatives having a direct effect on native people, women, the handicapped, new Canadians, as well as older workers.
Bill C-21 would also help young Canadians by improving entry-level skills development.
Under the Labour Force Development Strategy, students could learn the basic skills needed to enter a complex and rapidly changing labour market.
Bill C-21 also provides for the allocation of several millions of dollars, including $50 million to the Community Futures Program so vitally important for the small communities and rural areas of this country.
In addition, under the Labour Force Development Strategy, the government wants to double the funds earmarked for the industry assistance program which helps employers and workers adjust to change.
Older workers, who find it particularly difficult to secure a new job, would also benefit, Madam Speaker, from this Labour Force Development Strategy. These workers would have access not only to other retraining

June 4, 1990
Supply
programs but also to $100 million in additional funding for training, if Bill C-21 is passed.
Of course, Bill C-21 would play a considerable role in changing the present unemployment insurance plan into a more constructive and effective tool that can help Canadians at a key turning point in their life.
Bill C-21, Madam Speaker, provides $1.4 billion taken from the $12-billion regular UI fund. This $1.4 billion is being re-allocated, $800 million for worker training and $600 for new services, including twice as much maternity leave, better training, UI benefits for people over 65 and other similar improvements for all Canadians.
If Bill C-21 is passed, some 60,000 people will be able to receive training while they collect UI benefits. This bill would release $350 million to give Canadians the skills they need to find challenging and lasting employment.
Moreover, additional funds would be available to help social assistance recipients escape the trap which social assistance benefits represent.
Yet, because of this non-elected Senate's fault, all these essential initiatives have been pending since January last, as well as the crucial training agreements between the federal and provincial governments.
Madam Speaker, this short summary of Bill C-21 should clearly demonstrate to all the Members of this House and to the Senate just how disastrous an additional delay could be.
This summary of Bill C-21 should also demonstrate how absurd the Hon. Member's motion is on the Senate's right to defeat any bill coming from the House of Commons. The expression "any bill" is vital, because it means the money bills as well as the other bills with no expenditures of funds.
That, Madam Speaker, is what the House of Commons cannot accept and has always rejected for the past 80 years. It is not merely an abstract constitutional issue; the very survival of our country is at stake. Yet, as Bill C-21 has made it plainly obvious, the Senate's interference with the rights and privileges of the House is leading this country straight to political stagnation and senseless waste.
Madam Speaker, it is not the first time that the Senate with a Liberal majority has blocked the progress of this government's bills.
Let us just think for instance of Bill C-22, the Pattent Act, as well as the Free Trade bill which forced the Government to call an election because the Senate was adamantly refusing to adopt it in an effort to block the free trade agreement. Other bills, such as the one dealing with day care have been blocked by the Senate. There was another bill for which a Member of the Senate felt the need to put his life on the line in an effort to stop the government from cutting Katimavik. Senator Jacques Hebert was ready to die to salvage Katimavik. And yet, today, there is not a single man or woman in Canada who remembers Katimavik. Nobody ever mentions it.
This gives you an idea how far some people will go when they are not accountable to the voters and when they are sure to collect their salaray. These people tend to abuse their power.
Mr. Speaker, is the Hon. Member aware that the amendments to Bill C-21 the Liberal Senators insist upon would mean $1,75 billion per year in additional costs for Canadian taxpayers?
Is the Hon. Member aware that by defeating Bill C-21 the Senate would cause the Canadian taxpayers to pay some $2 billion in additional costs?
Is the Hon. Member who moved this motion aware that the proposed amendments would cause an imbalance in the Ways and Means approved by this duly elected House of Commons?
How can anyone be so stubborn, confused and irresponsible to come up with such a motion? If we are completely incapable of answering the hon. member from the New Democratic Party, I am confident that my constituents will remind him that the elected representatives of the people are expected to account for the use made of public money.
Those are its rights, Mr. Speaker, by virtue of the Constitution and of our own rules, as well as by centuries of parliamentary tradition during which precedents, practices and decisions have confirmed that the House of Commons is responsible for government finance matters.
It stands to reason, even for Canadians who oppose Bill C-21 but who have not given up on the underlying principles of the Constitution in a futile effort to gain short term support and who are appalled to see the Liberal dominated Senate, which is not even elected, throw sand in the democratic machine.
June 4, 1990

If anyone needed further evidence of the intellectual depth the NDP has reached, here it is. As I said, Mr. Speaker, I am curious to see how the members from the Liberal Party will vote on this motion. That should be something to see.
Maybe we will see them do a "flip flop", like some candidates to the direction of the party are doing regarding their position on the Meech Lake Accord. One day, they are against the agreement as it stands, but toward the end of the race, they start mellowing. Flip one way, flop the other way. That is interesting.
The member opposite suggests, let us not forget it, that the Senate has the power and the right to defeat any bill as it pleases. That is what it says. Members of this House will not be surprised to hear such a statement from a member of the New Democratic Party, because many of them doubt that party is committed to the principles it claims to defend.
What a shock it must be for other members of this House who believed the NDP was committed to democratic principles.
The opposition's statement is also preposterous, Mr. Speaker, because it applies to any bill even those our country needs the most. Legislation that could help the unemployed, Canadian workers, people on welfare, older workers and those who would like to get better training, as I say, any bill!
A vote for the motion of the New Democratic Party would be the equivalent of transferring our powers as elected representatives to the Upper House, to people who have not been duly elected by the people. To vote for such a motion would even mean renouncing our responsibilities and it would be a nonsense.
Bill C-21 is such a measure and its basic principle, training UI recipients with UI funds, has the support- Listen to this, opposition members. According to a Decima poll published on May 14, Bill C-21 was supported by two thirds of Canadians. Therefore, the hon. member does not seem to care about the needs or desires of the people with respect to this bill, if we go by his motion.
According to this motion, centuries of parliamentary tradition count for nothing. But the case that concerns us
Supply
today involves more than disrespect for parliamentary tradition; it shows disrespect for Canadians who expect all elected members of this House to do their job, which is to govern the country.
That is exactly what the government is trying to do with our bill and the Labour Force Development Strategy is a key element. Mr. Speaker, we are convinced that Canadians agree with us on these matters. If they do not, they can withdraw their support from us, unlike the senators, at the next election. That is how parliamentary democracy should operate. Only the elected members of this House and not the senators are answerable to the Canadian people. Suggesting that it might be otherwise, as the motion under consideration does, is unacceptable for all who firmly believe in the integrity of our political system and our democracy.
Mr. Speaker, I know that my time has already expired, but I think that it is important today to tell this House that the motion before us is unacceptable and that it should never even have been introduced. I think it is irresponsible to Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member opposite is a valued member of the House of Commons. He has ample experience in the business of the House and, to some degree I suppose, in the business of the other place. He has, I think, properly described the substance of the motion put forward by the New Democratic Party as being ill-founded and in many ways misconstruing the role and function of the Senate in Parliament.
In criticizing the New Democratic Party and others in such a way as to perhaps make the other place the whipping boy of Canadian parliamentary democracy, the member has failed to touch upon constructive initiative for reform of the Senate, which I think almost everyone in this House agrees should be initiated.
I know the hon. member will say that Senate reform is a viable, legitimate item on any reform agenda in this House and in the other place, but that perhaps some of us would prefer to postpone it until after June 23.
I suggest that the reform of the Senate is a very important issue. It is certainly a big enough issue to consume us here this afternoon.

June 4, 1990
Supply
I would like the hon. member to address, if he could, the initiatives that his government is prepared to take in terms of suggesting reforms and commencing a true debate aimed at reform of the other place.

Mr. Speaker, first of all, to respond to the hon. member's comment about initiatives for Senate reform, I may point out that at this very moment, 11 First Ministers are meeting a few streets down to try and ratify the Meech Lake Accord, which was duly signed three years ago by 11 First Ministers, with five minimum conditions, to get Quebec back in the Canadian Constitution. The first step towards Senate reform is to make Quebec part of the Constitution, a full-fledged member of the present Canadian federation.
Until Quebec is back in the constitutional fold, any future reform of the Constitution will be practically impossible. Mr. Speaker, Senate reform is necessary, and I think all of us here in the Flouse have seen for ourselves, what is happening to our bills and how the Senate is holding them up, and I think we all realize how pressing and urgent this reform has become. As you know, within our country, various First Ministers have entirely divergent views on what the Senate reform should be. You may have heard some Ministers talk about the Triple-E Senate. You may have heard other ministers saying it should be different. Our first step, however must be to bring Quebec back into the Constitution and make people understand that Quebecers within Canada form a distinct society, and it is that major step that must now be taken by all eleven First Ministers, and three in particular.
Senate reform will be next on the menu because, as we all know, Meech Lake provides for annual constitutional conferences. And I wish the hon. member would make it clear to one of his party's leadership candidates who is now playing with our country's future to clean up his act and send messages to Mrs. Carstairs, Mr. Wells and Mr. McKenna that they must approve Meech Lake as is. That would be an excellent thing to do for Canada, to make this leadership candidate, who is flip-flopping all over the place, understand that Canada is far more important than his own political aspirations.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to participate in the debate on this motion concerning the Senate. I can only say how amazed I am that the New Democratic Party would put forward this kind of silly nonsense in a motion. No one can dispute that the motion is correct. But the fact that the New Democratic Party, of all parties in Canada, would today come up with a motion urging the Senate in effect to exercise its undoubted constitutional rights and powers is simply beyond belief.
I took a look at some old speeches made by New Democratic Party members in the past. I want to remind the House of some of the words that have been uttered in this very Chamber by some predecessors of the current membership of that party. Some of those people would be absolutely astounded that their party was putting forward such a silly motion as this today for discussion in this House.
Some of the members must be ashamed even now. I am sure that someone in the leadership of the party got away from things on Friday afternoon and this silly motion got stuck on the Order Paper so that it could be discussed in this House. Now they have got themselves in a bit of a jam.
Let me read from April 6, 1964, as reported at page 1804 of Hansard. I have here a speech made by Mr. Stanley Knowles. I notice that that gentleman, who is normally sitting in this Chamber, has absented himself today. I can understand that when he would have had to listen to the drivel that we had to listen to from the hon. member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca when he was making his speech earlier. He was trying to cover all bases at once, as these New Democrats are wont to do.
Mr. Knowles on this day in 1964 had brought in a bill to abolish the Senate and he stated:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to implement the fundamental principle of democracy that the laws of a country should be made only by the elected representatives of the people. Its aim is to remove the possibility of the legislation enacted by the elected representatives being interfered with or delayed by a body of persons which has no mandate from the people of this country. The Senate being such a body this bill proposes its abolition.
That is what Mr. Knowles said in 1964.
June 4, 1990

I have more. In 1965, Mr. Howard, who was then a member of the New Democratic Party caucus, and as I recall the member for Skeena if I am not mistaken in my recollection, went on to discuss the votes for Estimates. The House was discussing Estimates and he was opposed to the Senate getting money. As reported at page 13154 of Hansard the former New Democratic Party member, Mr. Howard, stated in 1965:
Mr. Chairman, before you put the question on this particular item -
It was the administrative vote on the Senate.
I should like to make a few comments. 11 applies to the operation of what is politely or impolitely, depending upon the mood of the individual, referred to as the other place. This has always seemed to me to be a strange way to refer to it and I prefer to refer to it as the Senate because that is what it is, and it is almost always referred to in that way.
The program of the New Democratic party, as was the case with our predecessor, the C.C.F., includes the abolition of the Senate. As that is one of the things we would like to see accomplished I cannot in conscience lend my support to the item before us for the simple reason that by so doing we would be running counter to our belief. We cannot support an item which tends to perpetuate a structure that we would like to see abandoned and cease to exist.
In 1971, as reported at page 10651 of Hansard, Mr. Knowles-and I stress his absence because of shame at this party introducing such a silly resolution-brought forward a motion and sought the unanimous consent of the House so that he could discuss a motion to abolish the Senate. He sought unanimous consent, but he did not get it.
As reported at page 10616 of Hansard on December 20, 1971, Mr. Broadbent, the former leader of that party on my left, came up with this point. He stated:
I will come quickly to the point. In view of the speed with which the Senate is processing the bill, would the Prime Minister take steps in the early future that would result in the abolition of this absurd and undemocratic institution?
I am sure those words were out of order, Mr. Speaker, and why he was not called to order on the point I do not know. But, nevertheless, it reflects the attitude of the party on my left.
On October 30, 1970, as reported at page 758 of Hansard, Mr. Knowles stated:
The hon. member is asking about some of my friends up there -
-referring to the Senate.

All their lives they have been in favour of abolishing the Senate, and I trust they still are. After they have been there a while they will probably be more in favour of doing so.
In other words, his attitude had not changed from 1964 to 1970. He still believed in the abolition of the Senate.
As reported in Hansard on June 4, 1971, Mr. David Orlikow, then member for Winnipeg North, moved that a special committee be established to look at the Senate. In the course of his speech, as reported at page 6396 he stated:
Mr. Speaker, it will come as no surprise to hon. members that I am personally of the view that the Senate plays no useful role in the political life of Canada and that it ought, therefore, to be abolished.
That was in 1971 and I can understand why the electors in Winnipeg in 1988 realized that they had been duped by the New Democratic Party. They threw them all out, and for the simple reason that these people say one thing and mean another.
On the one hand, they say that the Senate is undemocratic and should be abolished, and on the other hand they say that the Senate, as undemocratic and bad as it is, should block these bills. That is what this motion we are debating today states. They are saying to us that we as a Liberal caucus ought to direct our Senate colleagues to block bills passed by this House.
It was not a matter of asking. The hon. member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca demanded that we do this and that we should insist that our caucus colleagues in the Senate block these bills.
We have never assumed such power over our Senate colleagues. Even before the last campaign when the former right hon. Leader of the Opposition, the member for Vancouver Quadra, asked the Senate to delay the free trade legislation so that the Canadian people could speak on the issue in an election, he did not demand or insist.
He instructed.

He asked. Read the press releases. He said to the Canadian people, "I have asked my colleagues in the Senate to hold up this bill". He did not say, ''I have instructed them". He did not say, "I demand that they do so". He is not Caesar. He is not the government House leader. He is a Liberal and he believes in the democratic principle, unlike the members of the New Democratic Party. They have stuck that name in their party's title to remind people that they are

democratic because they are so undemocratic in their activities.

An excellent motion.

(Edmonton East) The party policy is exactly the same.

As reported at page 11075 of Hansard for May 7,1990, the hon. member for Kamloops stated:
New Democrats watched intently the assault on democracy which took place last year-
Now they are participating in it, but we will leave that aside.
We exercised our democratic rights within our own party and voted at our December convention to change our party policy on the Senate. Whereas once we were satisfied that the Senate had to be abolished, and that was it, we are now in the process of looking at a variety of options to provide and promote better regional representation in the Parliament of Canada, including but not limited to, proportional representation, an elected Senate, and other options.
Ho, ho, ho, Christmas time was good to the New Democrats. They got off the hook. They got rid of their policy of abolishing the Senate. Then they come up with this kind of silly motion in June. Six months later they have scrapped all their principles, they have scrapped all their policies and they have gone the non-democratic route. It is not the New Democratic Party, it is the non-democratic party of Canada we are dealing with in this House today.
hear, hear!

I do not want the government members to think that I am defending their position in this matter. I hear applause from the other side. Of course they have no respect for the Senate. At least we in the Liberal party hold the senators with reverence and awe; experienced, seasoned politicians who have participated in the democratic process in this House and elsewhere in Canada, who have the capacity for sober second thought and the opportunity to review and pick up faults and errors in government legislation.
We do not urge on them the stopping of bills. We do not say that the Senate should can these bills. We recognize that the elected majority in the House of Commons has its responsibility and it fulfils that responsibility. But, when it comes down to it, we expect that there will be amendments sent back from the other place that may make significant change in some of those bills, because certainly many of the bills this government introduces are seriously flawed.
We try to point out the faults in this Chamber. Sometimes we are successful and sometimes we are not. With the majority the government has, if it is as pigheaded as it often is, it votes these bills through. The Senate then is left to try to pick up the pieces. At least we do not, like the New Democratic Party, urge the willy-nilly defeat of bills in the Senate, saying that the Senate ought to cross the will or wish of this House as

expressed by the elected representatives of Canadians, and that I think that is significant.
Let me go on with some of the other quotes from some other members of the New Democratic Party, because there are so many. In 1985, the hon. member for Oshawa again made comments about the Senate.

I believe it was during the March 5, 1985 Question Period, on page 2741. Mr. Broadbent asked the following question, an I quote:
Mr. Speaker, given the views of the Minister of Justice -I am trying to be very temperate -on this institution, and the well known views of the Deputy Prime Minister and, I dare to say, hopefully half of the Cabinet, not to mention 80 per cent of the people of Canada who correctly see the Senate as being useless and costly simultaneously, and since it takes the same section of our Constitution to abolish the Senate as it does to provide any other amendment of substance, will the Prime Minister give us his assurance today that he will propose to the provinces the correct, democratic action, which is to abolish this abominable insitution?
In light of such remarks concerning the Senate, Mr. Speaker, I am fascinated by the thought that the New Democratic Party would support a motion such as the one we are considering this afternoon. On January 23, 1981, as recorded on page 6533 of Hansard, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, said something else in a debate on the length of the senatorial mandate, and I quote:
- that there is no place in our parliamentary democracy for a body that is not elected, not responsible to anyone and that as the Senate now stands it should be abolished.
Hear, hear!

The hon. member for Edmonton East applauds and yet his party has changed that position. I presume he was in the minority that opposed the change in the position at the convention. I do not know how that all got away from the New Democratic Party at that time.

What is the Liberal
policy?

The image of overpaid Liberal and Conservative fund raisers, campaign managers and defeated or retired candidates who "work"-and I put that word in quotation marks-three days a week and do very little of value, is not too far from the truth. He would clearly disagree with this motion. He would not have supported this based on his previous statements in 1985. The hon. member for-
On a point of order, the hon. member for Edmonton East.

Other than that, the hon. member will have his time extended by 30 seconds.

It was a phoney point of order, Mr. Speaker, but I appreciate the hon. member's concern. It gave me an opportunity to have a drink of water. Now we have that same party saying that this undemocratic institution should block government bills. I could read the statement of the leader of the New Democratic Party which spouted this heresy in Montreal, but I think it would be wasting the time of the House to come out with that.
I have another authority that I want to quote. I want to cheer up the government benches with this one because it is written by one of their own senators. In case the government feels that it ought to ignore the Senate or that the Senate is not doing the constitutionally right thing, I want to read from one of its appointees to the Senate, the Hon. Gerald Beaudoin who has written a book-

La Constitution du Canada.
In fact, I believe he is considered as the government expert's in the other place on constitutional matters and powers of the Senate.
I have read some of the speeches he has made in the other place and I must say that if he is their constitutional expert, I wonder about the value of his book because his arguments in the Senate concerning constitutional and procedural matters are somewhat questionable.

With these three qualifications, the Upper Chamber enjoys the same powers as the elected House of Commons. Theoretically, it can even reject a budget or any ordinary legislation.

I see the hon. government House leader is nodding his agreement with his colleague in the Senate. Here we have notice given by the hon. member for Kamloops, the House leader of the New Democratic Party in this House, of a motion to reduce the Senate's program expenditures. It states:

expenditures, in the Main Estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1991.
Here he is calling on the Senate to block the bills, and then on the other hand he wants to take away their money. How inconsistent can you be? The New Democratic Party has to make up its own mind. It has to make up its mind which way it is going. Either support the Senate and say that it is an important part of our Parliamentary government, or else abolish it. They cannot have it both ways. This motion indicates that they are trying to have it both ways.

All aids and supplies granted to the Sovereign by the Parliament of Canada are the sole gift of the House of Commons, and all bills for granting such aids and supplies ought to begin with the House, as it is the undoubted right of the House to direct, limit, and appoint in all such bills, the ends, purposes, considerations, conditions, limitations and qualifications of such grants, which are not alterable by the Senate.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the government House leader has raised a very good point. I had my book open at Standing Order 80, but I ran out of time in my 20-minute speech and I could not get to this point.

I am delighted to have the opportunity to say that it is quite fortuitous that he has pulled out this rule and read it to the House. I need not read it again. Certainly the rule is one that we in this party have supported, as the hon. member knows.
He knows that on Bill C-21 for example, we argued vigorously that the bill was not one affecting aids and supplies and that therefore the amendments were in order. He will recall that discussion. I am glad he has raised it again today. I hope he now agrees with our position on that.
In any event, it is quite true that the situation is covered in Standing Order 80(1) and 80(2). I am tempted to read Standing Order 80(2) to the House. I may in a minute. It clearly indicates that this House in terms of money bills and in terms of bills that grant aids and supplies to the sovereign-and taxation falls into that category-are ones that are not alterable by the Senate.
Standing Order 80(2) says:
In order to expedite the business of Parliament, the House will not insist on the privilege claimed and exercised by them of laying aside bills sent from the Senate because they impose pecuniary penalties nor of laying aside amendments made by the Senate because they introduce into or alter pecuniary penalties in bills sent to them by this House; provided that all such penalties thereby imposed are only to punish or prevent crimes and offences, and do not tend to lay a burden on the subject, either as aid or supply to the Sovereign, or for any general or special purposes, by rates, tolls, assessments or otherwise.
In other words, the House tries to co-operate with the Senate when it does propose reasonable amendments to government bills. Certainly we feel that the amendments proposed by the Senate to Bill C-21, for example, are reasonable. I want to take the opportunity to do that. I know the government House leader does not share my view, but I hope he is coming around.
However, with respect to the motion that is before us, we have what the New Democratic Party is suggesting in a statement by its leader, of all people. Obviously the others on the front bench are not particularly supportive of that, except the hon. member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca. The message from their leader is that the Senate should stop the GST legislation, and that is what I find so extraordinary. This appears to be what is intended to be stated in the resolution.
While the difference of opinion there may be very great between the New Democratic Party and us on one hand and the government on the other, we as Liberals at least recognize that the majority wins the day in the House. We have not demanded, as has been suggested by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca, that our Liberal senators block this bill. We have said: "Look at it. Study it. You may end up blocking it, but it is your decision to that extent." Certainly we hope some amendments will be considered to this legislation that will make it less pernicious.
We would like to see the legislation done away with. We have urged the government to stop it. Through petition and through speech in the House, we have urged the government to stop it. We have been deprived in large measure of our opportunity to discuss the bill as a result of the tactics adopted by the New Democratic Party in stalling the House so that we could not have free debate and discussion.
Madam Speaker, you know this. The hon. government House leader knows it. We are all aware that there has been a real attempt here to stifle discussion in the House to prevent the Liberal party from expressing the valid criticisms of the legislation. Madam Speaker, I would like to ask a short question of the hon. member who contributed so magnificently to this debate. I just want to put the proposition to him that what we are doing in this debate is killing two birds with one stone. We can serve the interests of the vast majority
of the Canadian people who have demonstrated over and over again that they want to axe the tax, kill the GST, by persuading the Senate to fulfil its constitutional authority and responsibilities, and to put up or shut up and earn its keep. We may then be able to serve their desires and interests while enlisting the Conservative Party to the cause that we have held for years and continue to hold, which is that the Senate ought to be abolished.
If we can accomplish those two things at once, we can give the friends of our colleagues in the Liberal Party to our right their well deserved reward and put them out to pasture, without having to pay for it, and still accomplish the objectives of Canadians and the long-held objective of the New Democratic Party to put an end to that body which has sat in the other place without making a major, concrete contribution to the body politic for many years.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate on a topic which makes me a little uncomfortable. I think that those who put forward the motion, in their eagerness to blacken the noble record of the Liberal Party, have decided to use the Senate as a vehicle to pretend to Canadians that the Liberal Party has failed to provide the leadership and the traditions that have assisted the country to address the challenges of this century.
We have all heard many references to a triple E Senate, one that would purportedly be equal, effective, and elected. I know what elected means. I do not know exactly what equal means. Equal to what? Are we talking about equality as between provinces? Are we talking about equality as between regions? There are many other aspects of the country at which we can also look for equality.
None of these concepts have ever been ironed out, analysed, and developed in a cogent and cohesive manner to allow the House and the party in power to put forward a proposal for reform that has a chance of succeeding.
By way of our Constitution, we have in effect divided the constitutional pie into a number of segments; some portions federal, other portions provincial. Each jurisdiction is supreme in its own field. There are a few areas of shared jurisdiction.
I have to note that no provincial legislature makes use of a second body in their parliamentaiy process, yet each province enacts legislation fully as important as that of the House of Commons. The House of Commons and
each legislature in its own field deals fully and completely with its own aspect of the constitutional field. That makes me wonder why a Senate has a role in Parliament. If the provinces can get along just fine without a Senate or an upper House, why can the House of Commons not get along without a Senate? I have not found an answer to that.
I cannot say that the Senate does not perform a reasonable and effective function in many of the tasks that it undertakes in dealing with legislation. It does initiate some pieces of legislation. I have seen Senators of great repute, great experience, and great intelligence undertake tasks of significance to the provinces that they represent and great importance to the country, and carry out those responsibilities with great effectiveness. They have made a significant contribution to the development of legislation and policy in the country.
Yet, members of the New Democratic Party come forward today with a motion that pretends to endorse the functions of the Senate. But they are not being honest with themselves and they are not being honest with the House. The entire thrust of the New Democratic Party, for as long as I can remember, has been to abolish, to kill, to trample, and to change things so rapidly that it is prepared to throw the baby out with the bath water. When has the New Democratic Party ever given the Senate any credit for any of the work it has done?
The only fault the Senate bears is that through tradition in Canada the Senate has not been an elected body. I suppose many of us regret that. If it were an elected body, we would not have so many of the difficulties we now have in trying to determine its proper role.
I have made reference to those non-policies and destructive suggestions of the New Democratic Party, which from time to time are rooted in real democratic initiative. However, I feel they fail to recognize some of the good things we have here in this country. Not only does the NDP take that approach, but the Progressive Conservative Party in its own way has also failed to address Senate reform in the way it should have.
The Progressive Conservative government over the last half dozen years has spent its time cutting deals with Washington rather than trying to reform and to improve mechanisms of legislation in Parliament. It abandoned the Senate long ago. It did not give a care about the
June 4, 1990

Senate. Its goals were expedience and quick fix. I am disappointed in that.
What we have to show for it is a half finished free trade agreement. I say half finished because we have not finished negotiating subsidy. We have a challenge of constitutional reform which has been left for three years. As I stand here, we are now negotiating-truly at the eleventh hour-to put together some rational constitutional reform which has emanated out of the Meech Lake Constitutional Accord.
I want to conclude by speaking in opposition to the adoption of the motion put forward by the New Democratic Party. It is a motion that is devoid of any real substance and any real constructive initiative to reform the Senate. It is one that attempts to show our party, a party that I am very proud of, as one that has not done the work that it was elected to do over the last several decades.
I challenge the NDP to abandon its bankrupt approach to Senate reform and address solid, positive, constructive constitutional and Senate reform in the months to come.

Madam Speaker, my friend has just exhorted the Liberals in this House to do with the Senate what the labour unions have been doing to the NDP for years, that is, telling the NDP what to do in the House of Commons. No one in the Liberal party in this House has stated what the Senate is going to do with the GST legislation. That is up to the Senate. Suggestions by the New Democratic Party that the Senate was either going to vote to kill it or do nothing are wrong. Madam Speaker, I have another question that I thought I might address to my hon. friend.
He will know that in the 17 years of Liberal administration from the 1960s through to 1984, when common sense prevailed, that the Senate under the control of the Liberal party used to indulge in pre-studies of bills in an effort to make the work of the House of Commons, the duly elected representatives, flow quickly once the bills got to the Senate. The Senate abandoned that once the Conservatives gained control of the House of Commons.
I wonder if my hon. friend could comment on what caused this change of policy in the Senate and whether or not he thinks it is legitimized at all.

Madam Speaker, it seems to me that if there existed a valid, workable, effective institution procedurally at the time that the Progressive Conservatives came into power in 1984, it would only seem appropriate that
they exercise leadership and judgment in pursuing that kind of a process. In fact, if that process fell into disuse, I would have to suggest that it was a result, not of the failure of the Senate which does not lead legislation in this country, but of the Progressive Conservative government to make use of processes and of an institution that had validity, and of people who had experience simply because it looked to them like the Senate was filled with Liberals and they did not like Liberals. So they stayed away and they failed to use a good procedure that was there in existence simply out of partisanship.

Madam Speaker, I would like to begin the approximately five minutes that are left to us in this evening's debate by reading the eloquent motion put forward by my colleague from Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca earlier this afternoon. It states:
That a message be sent to the Senate reminding the Senate-
And it needs reminding.
- that it has the constitutional right and the power to defeat any bill coming from the House of Commons.
At the beginning of this debate my colleague from Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca made it abundantly clear why this particular language was used. We have been listening for months now to representatives of the Liberal party railing against the goods and services tax, this aberration of progressive taxation from one end of Canada to the other. Quite frankly, we thought it was time to call their bluff.
The Constitution says that the Senate has that authority, it has that power and it has that responsibility. We in the New Democratic Party have said for years that it ought not to have that power but the fact remains that it does have it. We also believe that we ought to get value for moneys expended. The long and excellent financial histories of NDP provincial governments across the country are adequate testimony to that.
What are you wasting money on this for?

We will debate that some other day but the press has already agreed that the facts are on my side and I will not deal with that any further right now. It is not necessary. The facts will speak for themselves.
By this motion we want to ensure that those thousands of Canadians who may appear before the Senate as it
June 4, 1990

travels from one end of the country to the other to hear testimony, give serious consideration and sober second thought to this question of the goods and services tax, this fundamental rearranging of Canada's taxation regime, know that it is a sham, that it does not mean a thing.
One after another my Liberal neighbours have stood up today and said they have no intention, either as Liberals or as members of a Liberal caucus, of having the Senate impose its will on the Parliament of Canada. So it is a non-starter.
To go back in history a little bit, the Senate was set up as the protector of corporate rights, the protector of private property against those radicals who wanted to democratize society. The Senate has many times in Canadian history used its power, its responsibility and its authority to stop good laws. We are asking the Liberal party to request their fellow Liberal caucus members to use their constitutional rights and authority within the Senate of Canada to put an end to a bad law.
In 1926 the old age pension bill was introduced by a Liberal government after the signed commitment received by J.S. Woodsworth and A.A. Heaps in 1921. It took them a little while but they brought in a bill and the action of the Senate was described as its most notorious act of defiance. The Senate killed the popular policy, the aim of which was to supplement the income of all people 70 years of age or over to $365 a year. The Senate killed a good law.
In 1926-27, the Senate twice rejected a bill to repeal section 41 of the Immigration Act, which permitted the deportation of British subjects not Canadian citizens without trial. The Senate feared its passage would encourage communist infiltration into Canada.
In 1926, 1927, 1928, 1929 and 1930 the Senate consistently refused to pass measures to repeal section 98 of the Criminal Code enacted in 1919 to deal with unlawful association. The majority of the Senate held that communism was still making headway in Canada and if the clause were repealed there would be no provision in the Code to deal swiftly with agitators seeking to overthrow the government. Those were provisions that were opposed by every Canadian who was concerned about civil rights. They stemmed from an incident in the Winnipeg general strike in 1919.
