Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise in this Chamber today to address a number of points which I believe are of critical importance, not only to my colleagues in this Chamber, but to the people of Canada.
Some of you will recall that I had asked when and why this Minister of Finance and his government decided to change their position on the reduction of the deficit, that is their position was predicated on the basis that they felt that there were other ways besides reducing transfer payments to health and education.
I want to quote what the minister said. In 1982, the Minister of Finance said:
The reductions to federal funding of health and education could have disastrous effects on the universities and on the colleges, on the hospital funding and on the operation of the hospitals. Let us solve those problems not on the backs of the hospitals and universities; let us solve those problems outside of that arena.
That is what the minister said then, but what is he doing now? Supposedly they were not going to touch that formula, supposedly not. They reduced it by 2 per cent in 1986 and they reduced it for two years. They have now frozen it from $86 to $95 billion. There will be $31 billion fewer dollars for health and education. That is just one reduction.
They have reduced funding for training and retraining when they said we would have the best programs in the world. They have done that on the backs of the workers and on the backs of the small business people and other business people of this nation. They have reduced the funding for science and technology by $39 million. You will recall that they said they would double research and development. It used to be at 1.40 per cent gross domestic productivity, half of what it is in the United

June 4, 1990
Adjournment Debate
States, Japan and a number of European nations. It is now 1.32. It has slipped even further.
The minister's response, I contend, is one that most individuals would agree to be somewhat misleading, to say the least. Some people would even say it is farcical. Some people have even told me it was somewhat machiavellian, but I wonder if it would not be better to say it is "Michaelvellian" or perhaps "Michaelvillain".
Let us go on to the second part of the question. The second question was would he please agree with me and confirm my contention that transferring cash and transferring tax points were actually quite different. Will the minister please tell the whole truth about cash and transfer payments? That is what I wanted to know.
He gave tax points away, or the government of the day did, 10 years ago and he is still claiming them for himself, for his government. They gave points, not dollars, and there is a difference. I can give you 100 points tonight but I must tell you it is not going to buy you a whole lot for dinner. The minister and his government take credit for points which were transferred over a decade ago, and yet the provinces raised the taxes. Surely that is something that needs to be said and a point that needs to be recognized.
During the last two years the tax point credits were greater than was the cash transfer. Manitoba will have no more cash from transfer payments for health and education by the year 2003 to 2004.1 think that is really quite unfortunate. This is what the minister said in response to my question, quite apart from being rather flippant and a lot of puffery surrounding all of this and I think rather insensitive: "The tax points and cash transfer are equally important to the provinces because in an equal way they provide cash to the provinces."
Here is what an expert, Tim Sale and Associates, from Winnipeg, Manitoba, had to say about tax points.
"Tax points" is jargon which means that the provinces got the right to levy higher rates of personal and corporate income tax in return for agreeing to the federal proposal. In turn, the federal rates were lowered. Provinces raised their personal income taxes by 12 points (each point is one per cent of the federal tax level), and their corporate rates by 1 point. The federal government
could still claim to be funding medicare, but at a lower direct cost to their budget each year. The political price for higher taxes was paid by the provinces.
I could go on and I shall use a couple of other quotes.
The federal government shifted some taxation to the provinces- gave provinces the right to raise their taxes. But the federal government still counts the money that is raised by those provincial tax points as federal dollars.
And it goes on and on and on. The point is a very simple one. The transfer of tax points is not the same as a tax transfer of cash. It is simply not the same. I thought the minister on that particular day had been somewhat arrogant, somewhat pretentious, somewhat pompous and insensitive to the point that I was trying to raise. If that minister discards what I am saying, let him consult with my experts. Let him consult with the Canadian Association of University Teachers, the Canadian Association of Community Colleges, and I could name several others. We can listen to what they have to say. I would be quite willing to settle with their conclusion.
If the minister is so sure of himself and the points that he makes, I wonder why he did not accept my October 13 challenge, which was to discuss the importance of education and transfer payments for health and education throughout the country. In an exchange here in the House one day, I said to the minister that I would love to debate this issue with him throughout Canada. He said he had checked Hansard and he could see no indication that he had undertaken to do that.
The points are very simple.

Madam Speaker, it is because I had adressed two extremely important issues. I was brushed off by the minister, and I believe he was less then honest with me and my collegues. Tonight, in the House, I ask that someone should explain to me why he believes he is right, when I contend I am the one who's right.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to respond to the hon. member's question that he put to the Minister of Finance on March 13, 1990.
June 4, 1990

This government inherited a large deficit, a debt problem, in 1984. The federal government at that time was living far beyond its means. It borrowed $16 billion just to cover the difference between the money spent on programs, services, and the revenues that were collected. It built up a $200 billion debt, a mountain of debt that generated more than $22 billion of annual interest charges.
When we came to power, we launched a broad and sustained attack to reduce expenditures and restore our fiscal house. This was part of a long-term plan. We terminated special tax breaks, closed loopholes and increased revenues. The results speak for themselves. We turned an operating deficit into an operating surplus of $10 billion. Progress on these programs of deficit reduction have been made and the growth of the federal program spending has been held below the rate of inflation.
As a share of the economy, our spending is at the lowest level in 20 years. But more needs to be done, we know that, because of the huge deficits built up before 1984. Public debt is still growing faster than the economy, faster than our ability to pay, and this year alone interest payments on our debt will cost almost $40 billion. That is 35 cents out of every dollar collected as federal revenue, or it means $1,500 for each Canadian.
The best way to reduce debt is to reduce spending. The federal transfers to provinces are simply too large to exempt from spending restraint. Major federal transfers to provinces have grown by 6.5 per cent annually over the last five years. This is well in excess of the 3.6 per cent average annual growth of federal program spending over this period. Cash transfers alone represent 24 per cent of total federal program spending.
Therefore, the budget proposes to hold per capita Established Programs Financing transfers constant for the next two fiscal years. Total transfers under the Establish Programs Financing arrangements will continue to grow with the population, or about 1 per cent annually.
The impact of this measure will be spread broadly and equitably across all provinces and will represent less than 1 per cent of provincial revenues.
Adjournment Debate
Federal program spending will increase about 3 per cent in 1990-91. Our transfers to provinces will also increase by about 3 per cent next year. So we are requiring no more of the provinces than we are willing to bear ourselves.
It is important to remember that in addition to Established Programs Financing, the federal government provides substantial additional assistance to the lower income provinces through the equalization program.
I want to mention particularly to the hon. member that this helps provinces provide better public services in health care and education and that equalization transfers have been exempted from the restraint measures announced in the budget.

Madam Speaker, on May 24, 1990 I asked a question of the Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport concerning the devastating effect the proposed goods and services tax will have on amateur sport in Canada, and in particular minor hockey.
The minister responded by saying that the Sports Federation of Canada is very pleased with the provisions of the GST to amateur sport. However, a report produced by Douglas A. Rollins of Nepean suggests that any provisions the government has put forward do not go far enough to address the problems of a GST on certain amateur sports in Canada.
To better provide evidence of my belief that the GST will have a negative effect on minor hockey in Canada, I will read verbatim from Mr. Rollins' paper:
This paper has been researched and prepared to assess the impact of the proposed Goods and Services Tax (GST) on local minor hockey associations across Canada, and of individual teams and officials operating in such an association. The purpose of the paper is to provide a clearer understanding of this tax, and to make recommendations as to how these associations could arrange their affairs so as to prepare for the GST.
This paper has been prepared as a "case study". It examines the operations of the Nepean Minor Hockey Association, and of the teams and officials in it. This was a deliberate choice, since by examining the GST and its impact upon one specific organization, other similar organizations would be able to clearly identify the underlying principles of law, and relate these principles to their own particular organization. This would then fulfil the objective of the paper, to provide a clearer understanding of this tax for all.

June 4, 1990
Adjournment Debate
Material was gathered through examination of existing federal sales tax law, through review of Bill C-62, an act to amend the Excise Tax Act, and discussions with officials of the Nepean Minor Hockey Association and tax policy officers with the Department of Customs and Excise, and Finance.
It must be clear at the outset that the material presented in this paper, because of the nature of the subject, cannot be considered as definite. This is because the goods and services tax has been introduced into the House of Commons as Bill C-62 but is not a law at this time. Also, in certain of the more technical aspects of the application of GST there is no policy. What is presented is the likely direction such policy will take. These areas of uncertainty have been identified in the body of the text.
Despite these considerations, what is presented here is the first detailed look at this tax and its specific implications for minor hockey.
I do not have the time to read the background and methodology of the report, but I will read the executive summary.
The GST is intended to eliminate many of the flaws and inequities which exist in the current Federal Sales rfax. The vast majority of goods and services in Canada will be subject to this tax, which is essentially a 7 per cent tax on personal consumption. It will require all businesses and organizations in Canada who have annual taxable sales in excess of $30,000 to register for and collect this tax.
The Nepean Minor Hockey Association, like all other hockey associations in Canada, will be affected by this tax. As the organization providing a minor hockey program for players between the ages of five and 19 in the city of Nepean, the NMHA in 1989-90 operated with a total budget of $402,000. The vast majority of these funds come from the sale of memberships to individual players. In addition, other revenue comes from the rental of practice ice purchased from the city, the proceeds from a bingo, profits from a used equipment sale, sponsor contributions and tournament revenues.
It is concluded that the NMHA, given its current operations, would have a total of $206,500 in taxable sales annually. This would require the NMHA to register for GST and collect some $14,020 in taxes yearly. However, by taking eligible input tax credits of $10,185, the net amount of GST to remit would be a total of $3,935. While the NMHA is a non-profit organization, it will receive no special funding, unlike certain other organizations engaged in organizing amateur athletics.
In addition to the amount of GST required to be added to its sales, the NMHA will be forced to absorb a total of $20,406 in GST on its purchases. As a consequence, the NMHA will face a total GST related increase of $24,341. This represents a 6 per cent increase.
There are ways of reducing the NMHA's total amount of taxable sales to less than $30,000 per year, but this would only save some
$3,935 in GST annually. This is due to the fact that the NMHA, being a non-profit organization, does not mark up purchases subsequently resold to any significant amount. By not being registered, by being below the $30,000 threshold, they would not have to keep books and records, and file periodic tax returns, but would save relatively little money.
Individual teams in the NMHA would not be registered for GST as long as their operating budget does not exceed $30,000. In a similar manner, referees, timekeepers and instructors would be below this threshold.
I filed a copy of this report with the Minister of Fitness and Amateur Sport at the time I asked the question. I hope the parliamentary secretary or whoever responds will have had the time to read the report and to specifically refer to the items that I mentioned.
This report was very well thought out and researched. Even after it took into account all the provisions that were supposed to help non-profit amateur sport, an increase of 6 per cent to an organization such as the NMHA still exists. This could have an extremely negative effect on minor hockey in Nepean and, as is probably the case, all of Canadian minor hockey.
In response to my initial question in the House, the Minister of Fitness and Amateur Sport praised the Minister of Finance for doing a tremendous job for amateur sport in the GST legislation and stated he should be congratulated. I say to the minister, come on. Put your helmet on and get into the game. Your praise of the Minister of Finance is eloquent but makes no sense. In hockey terms, you do a lot of dazzling skating and shooting but no scoring.
Your answers to my questions deserve a misconduct and I am sure you will be cut from the team when Canadians vote in the next election.

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to respond to the hon. member's concerns.
I want to make very clear that the Government of Canada has no intention of scrapping the goods and services tax. We all know the GST is an important part of the government's economic plan. It is a crucial element that contributes to making the economy stronger and more dynamic, to restoring the country's financial health, and to improving the fairness of the tax system.
June 4, 1990

The proposed tax will correct many of the flaws of the existing federal sales tax. It will remove the existing tax burden from many Canadian exports, eliminating the bias in favour of imports by applying a uniform tax rate to imports and domestic goods and services. It will provide a more reliable source of revenue and thereby contribute to efforts to reduce the national deficit.
With a uniform rate of 7 per cent applied to most goods and services, the GST will provide a less complex system for government and businesses to administer. In strengthening the competitive position of Canadian producers, the GST will stimulate economic growth, encourage investment, and create jobs.
Insofar as the amateur sport community is concerned, let me remind hon. members that non-profit organizations as a whole are not now given special status under the existing FST. As a consequence, such organizations currently bear an element of sales tax on their purchases, which presumably they are required to factor in to the cost of the programs they provide.
In developing the GST proposal, the government recognized that, given the broader GST base, such organizations would generally incur additional costs. As a result, important features of substantial benefit to charities and non-profit organizations have been incorporated into the proposed system.
First, government grants or subsidies available to charitable and non-profit organizations in order to carry out their activities are not taxed. They are ignored for GST purposes.
Second, charitable and non-profit organizations which produce taxable supplies will be able to claim full input tax credits on their purchases.
Third, to further mitigate the impact of the GST, charities-and this includes registered Canadian amateur athletic associations-will automatically be entitled to a 50 per cent rebate on GST paid on purchases for non-commercial use, regardless of the amount of funding they receive from governments. Organizations which do not have charitable status, but which nonetheless are substantially funded non-profit organizations, that is, those whose revenues comprise at least 40 per cent in
Adjournment Debate
government funding, will also be able to claim a 50 per cent rebate of GST on purchases of goods and services for which they are not entitled to an input tax credit. This places them in a better position than under the current federal sales tax.
There are a number of other features which have been built in to the design which will benefit sport and other non-profit organization. Among others, these include the provision of an optional simplified accounting method to reduce any additional compliance burden, the exemption of sponsorships from tax, and a special exemption for recreational programs designed for children primarily under the age of 14.
The former Minister of State for Fitness and Amateur Sport helped to facilitate representations by the Sport Federation of Canada before the Commons Finance Committee last fall and also facilitated key meetings between that organization and the Department of Finance. At the present time, officials of the Fitness and Amateur Sport Branch are working with the Sports Federation and Revenue Canada to ensure as smooth an implementation of the GST for the sport and fitness communities as possible.

Madam Speaker, I rise as chairman of the Public Accounts Committee to raise an item once again that was first raised in the House on October 23, 1989.
The purpose of the Public Accounts Committee is to study, as thoroughly as it can, the annual report of the Auditor General of Canada tabled in the House each year during October or November. It is the committee's job to study the items in that report where the Auditor General finds weaknesses in financial administration or areas of government that should be corrected. We have hearings and, after those hearings with civil servants and senior officials from government departments and agencies before us, we table our report in the House, not only stating our findings, but also making recommendations on the cures.
On October 23,1 raised an issue in the House because the Deputy Prime Minister had sent out letters to all the chairmen of committees of the House of Commons, asking them for suggestions as to how the deficit could

June 4, 1990
Adjournment Debate
be decreased. But he forgot to send one to the chairperson of the Public Accounts Committee.
I raised that in a question in the House and the Deputy Prime Minister gave me a very good answer. He said he was willing to co-operate with us. In a second question to him, I said the Auditor General's report will be tabled in the House tomorrow and it will be permanently referred to the Public Accounts Committee. I asked if he would assure us that no roadblocks will be put in the committee's way as we witnessed, to a degree, in the early stages of this Parliament. The Auditor General's Report was tabled the next day on October 24, and these points were raised:
In 1989-90 we had planned to conduct a government-wide audit of expenses claimed by ministers for travelling on government business. In our opinion, the Auditor General has clear statutory authority to audit these expenses.
The Auditor General went on to say in his report:
We requested access to receipts where ministers had followed Treasury Board's advice to retain them. The Government told us that even if receipts existed they would not be made available to us.
In other words, the government refused access to those ministerial receipts to the Auditor General of Canada who looks after tax moneys given to the government on behalf of the people of Canada.
On October 24 in the House, I rose again and said:
Today we learned that the Auditor General tried to do an audit on ministerial travel, but he could not perform it because he could not get any receipts from any ministers in this government and therefore could not do an audit of the cabinet of this country. Surely the Deputy Prime Minister does not consider this to be co-operation.
The President of the Treasury Board replied:
I can assure you that this government is totally committed to accountability and openness.
Madam Speaker, on November 10 in The Globe and Mail there is a report of one of the public accounts committee meetings and it states:
Paul Tellier, Clerk of the Privy Council and secretary to the cabinet, testified yesterday before the House of Commons public accounts committee that the Auditor-General of Canada will not have access to receipts for government-paid trips taken by ministers.
He said it is up to each minister to decide how to spend his or her time and it is not the role of the Auditor General to pass judgement on where the minister goes or why.
That was not really the purpose of it. It was a request for information for the purpose of bringing forward an audit.
Time went by and the President of the Treasury Board gave us a commitment that he would bring back a report on this.
On February 8, not having a report, I wrote to the President of the Treasury Board and asked him for his report. I said:
At a meeting of the Committee with the Comptroller General on February 8,1990, it was brought to our attention that two reports on the above subject are presently in your hands, one is entitled: "Report to the President of the Treasury Board on the accounting for the Administrative Flight Service provided by the Department of National Defence"; the other is a report on ministerial travel.
We asked the President of the Treasury Board for that information. He replied to my February 8 letter on March 13. He said:
The Comptroller General's study has been provided to me just recently and is presently under consideration. As you know, I promised to table this document in the House and will do so early in the new fiscal year. At that time, it will be available to the Public Accounts Committee.
In other words, Madam Speaker, hurry up and wait. On January 17, I received a letter from the Auditor General. I will quote a paragraph from that as follows:
I thought your Committee might appreciate knowing that the government of the Province of Manitoba has very recently moved away from an honour system for accounting for ministerial travel expenses to a system requiring receipts. The significance of this development is that it leaves the government of Canada as the sole jurisdiction where Ministers' travel expenses are accounted for on an honour basis, i.e. receipts are not required.
It is now June 4. Parliament will be rising this month. This issue that started on October 24 last fall and our public accounts committee still does not have an answer from the President of the Treasury Board. We still do not have an answer from the government.
Madam Speaker, I want to state very clearly that the public accounts committee studying matters of inefficiency and bad expenditures in government can only operate if we get the full co-operation of the government. I want to point out, as chairman of the public accounts committee, it is obvious that on this item we are not getting co-operation, either from a senior official or from the government itself. I would like the government to tell us why and when we are going to get it.
June 4, 1990

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would first like to point out to the hon. member that when he raised this question on October 23, the Deputy Prime Minister did apologize to him for not sending a letter and wanted to assure us that the government wants the public accounts committee to be the watch-dog committee of the public purse.
As well, the committee can expect the same freedom and independence it has always exercised. Furthermore, as the committee continues to fulfil its important role, we would welcome any ideas, suggestions or otherwise to assist the government and the country in reducing its national debt.
I know the hon. member shares the view that we must find ways to reduce duplication in government and to find efficient methods to meet the program demands of Canadians. We as a government are constantly searching for ways to improve the delivery of programs. But, as he well knows, when an operation the size of the federal government spends approximately $100 billion annually, it has an obligation and a duty to promote efficiency in our spending.
The Public Accounts Committee, which the hon. member chairs, is tasked with reviewing federal govern-
Adjournment Debate
ment spending and with providing alternative ideas and new opportunities. I know the hon. member will be doing just that.
Elowever, we should take time to look at our record. If we take away government spending to service the Liberal national debt, we will find that that the government has gone from a $16 billion operating deficit in 1984-85 to a $25 billion operating surplus in 1990-91.
That sounds impressive. The deficit will drop to $28.5 billion this year. It will be cut to $14 billion in three years and reduced further to $10 billion in the next years.
Given these facts, I want to congratulate the Public Accounts Committee for its hard work in helping to achieve this impressive turn-around. In the same view, I know the hon. member who chairs the Public Accounts Committee would want to congratulate the government for providing leadership in getting government spending under control.
